#7463. Trump administration brings White House ballroom battle back to Supreme Court

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court last week, once again asking the justices to intervene in its ongoing efforts to build a new White House ballroom. On Aug. 31, a divided court paused a ruling by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., that would have halted above-ground construction on the project. In a petition filed on Nov. 5, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the court to reverse the lower court’s ruling outright or to take up the case and hear oral arguments on the merits. He told the justices that their earlier ruling “has all but answered the question presented” by the dispute, and that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”

Construction on the project began in October of last year with the demolition of the East Wing. In December, the National Trust for Historic Preservation – a private nonprofit that describes itself as having “led the movement to save America’s historic places” “[f]or more than 75 years” – filed a lawsuit in federal court, seeking to block the construction until the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts could review the plans for the construction; the NCPC could approve those plans; and Congress could authorize the construction.

To support its argument that it had a legal right to sue, known as standing, the trust submitted a declaration from Alison Hoagland, a member who lives in Washington, D.C., and said that she visits the area where the White House is located approximately once per month. Hoagland, who has “expertise in historic architecture,” claimed that the project caused “‘injuries’ to her ‘aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests’ because she finds the ‘scale,’ ‘height,’ and ‘massing’ of the government’s design distasteful.”

Senior U.S. District Judge Leon issued an order in late March that temporarily barred the construction of the ballroom above ground but allowed underground construction – of, for example, bomb shelters and bunkers – to move forward, along with any above-ground construction necessary for safety and security.

Before Leon’s ruling could go into effect, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit froze it to give that court time to consider the government’s appeal. In August, a divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld Leon’s ruling but delayed its effective date for 14 days to allow the federal government to go to the Supreme Court.

Writing for the majority, Judges Patricia Millett and Bradley Garcia emphasized that Congress, and only Congress, has the power “to regulate the construction and demolition of White House structures,” but it has not approved any money for the ballroom construction.

In her dissent, Judge Neomi Rao contended (among other things) that the trust did not have a legal right to bring a lawsuit, known as standing, to try to stop the ballroom construction.

Calling Leon’s ruling “extraordinary and unlawful,” the Trump administration came to the court on its interim docket on Aug. 13. Sauer asked the justices to temporarily pause Leon’s ruling, telling them that it would “halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security.” He argued that the trust lacks standing to sue, because its claims rest on a member’s “dislike” for the new construction – which, it said, is not the kind of injury that would allow the lawsuit to go forward.

On Aug. 21, the day that Leon’s order was scheduled to go into effect, Chief Justice John Roberts issued an administrative stay – that is, an order that kept Leon’s order on hold (and permitted construction to continue) – to give the justices additional time to consider the government’s request.

By a vote of 5-4, the court on Aug. 31 granted the government’s application and continued the pause on Leon’s order. In an eight-page, unsigned opinion, the majority stressed that it was not deciding whether the project was legal. Instead, it said, the trust likely lacks standing to challenge the project at all. The harms that Hoagland alleges, the majority wrote, are not the kind of “concrete” and specific injuries required to bring a lawsuit. Moreover, the majority said, if Leon’s order were allowed to go into effect, the government would be permanently harmed – another key criterion in determining whether to grant emergency relief. Among other things, it noted, senior government officials “attest[] that constructing something approximating the height and mass of the intended above-ground ballroom is ‘crucial’ to the security of the below-ground military installation.”

Roberts dissented, in an opinion joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson. In his view, the construction “is likely unlawful,” and the majority’s decision was “no victory for the separation of powers.” He contended that the trust did have standing to sue because “[a] historic preservationist such as Hoagland can be aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys, just as,” based on prior court precedent, “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys.”

In its Nov. 5 petition, the Trump administration argued that “the East Wing renovation is a vital national-security effort taking place on the White House grounds with the President’s personal involvement,” and that it has “proceeded swiftly since construction began in October 2025, in keeping with the urgency of remedying the East Wing’s obsolete and vulnerable security infrastructure, all as this President faces an onslaught of assassination attempts.” Because Leon’s order blocked the project “at the behest of a single passerby who complains that she expects to dislike its ultimate design,” Sauer wrote, his “decision is demonstrably flawed.”

Sauer acknowledged that the court’s Aug. 31 ruling came on the interim docket and therefore “only involve[d] a preliminary look at the merits and equities” of the dispute. But, he continued, in this case “[t]here is nothing further or new that this Court needs to decide after its” earlier opinion “in order to answer the question presented” by the government’s new filing – specifically, whether Leon was wrong to block “the ongoing renovation of the East Wing of the White House.” This is especially true, Sauer suggested, given the court made its Aug. 31 decision “after extensive briefing, and issue[d] detailed majority and dissenting opinions addressing” the issues in the case.

Sauer urged the court to summarily reverse Leon’s decision – that is, to reverse it without additional briefing or oral argument – or, at a minimum, grant review and hear oral arguments.

The trust’s response to the government’s petition is currently due on Dec. 7.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7461. PubMatic Is All In On Agentic Buys; How Much Power Is Too Much Power?

PubMatic saw sizable growth in Q3, with its revenue totaling $79.6 million – up 17% from the same period last year.

Its not-so-secret sauce? Advancing AI solutions and increased demand for CTV and mobile app advertising.

CTV spend represented 21% of PubMatic’s total revenue this quarter, up 30% year over year, CFO Steve Pantelick told investors on Monday afternoon’s earnings call. Mobile app revenue grew even faster, nearly 40% year over year, and made up roughly 27% of quarterly revenue.

But it’s not just ad spend that’s evolving; it’s how the ads are bought and launched. Since PubMatic launched AgenticOS, its operating system for agentic advertising, in January, buyers have used it to run over 120 fully agentic campaigns, roughly one-third of which happened in Q3.

And the company only expects that number to go up.

When asked by an investor what parts of a campaign are still done by humans and which steps can’t be replicated by AI, PubMatic CEO Rajeev Goel suggested that whatever isn’t yet being done by AI soon will be.

Some clients are “all in on AI,” while others want to manually review each step of the campaign, Goel said, describing it as different “parts of the maturity spectrum.”

Meaning: If you don’t want AI doing your work for you, tough luck. Just “mature” a few more years.

“There’s a lot of risk in automating choice,” Jonathan Roberts, head of innovation at People Inc., cautioned listeners during the IAB roundtable discussion “Advertising in the Agentic Era” on Monday.

Although allowing an AI assistant to make purchase decisions may be a tempting convenience, it will devolve into a “winner takes all” situation for brands, which is, simply put, “bad for democracy,” said Roberts.

Not to mention the fact that what’s best for one customer isn’t best for everyone. Roberts likens AI answer engines to a bar where every customer is handed an espresso martini because that’s the average, or most common, order.

Otherwise, said Roberts, “we have this kind of ‘espresso martini for everyone’ world, and that sucks.”

WPP-owned ad agency Ogilvy is partnering with Creative Artists Agency (CAA) to use the likenesses of CAA’s celebrity clients in AI-generated ads, reports Digiday.

The resulting ads will use data from CAA’s library of digital face and body scans, which it already maintains for use in deaging and postproduction work. They will also be watermarked as AI and approved by the talent featured therein.

Technically, this agreement is a kosher one as far as Hollywood is concerned. SAG-AFTRA’s AI regulations stipulate that performers are required to give consent to the use of digital replicas and must be compensated at the same rates as they would be for in-person filming.

But even though actors are on board (although only Terry Crews has publicly opted in so far), it might still be difficult for consumers to come around to the idea of AI-generated endorsements.

Sure, AI-generated content is now prevalent enough that some audience members are even voluntarily watching it. (Remember how many views “Fruit Love Island” got?) But the existing association that many users probably still have between deepfaked celebrity endorsements and online scam ads might be tougher to overcome.

#7459. Court appears unlikely to side with inmate in lawsuit for violation of his constitutional rights

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Monday appeared to side with a prison paramedic in a lawsuit brought by an inmate who contends that the paramedic’s failure to provide medical treatment violated his constitutional rights. During just over 80 minutes of oral argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, a majority of the justices seemed poised to throw out the inmate’s lawsuit, even if it wasn’t clear whether they were ready to bar such lawsuits more broadly in the future.

The inmate, Kekai Watanabe, was seriously injured in a gang-related fight while he was in a federal detention center in Hawaii. He says that he told Francis Nielsen, a paramedic who treated him, that his pain was severe, but he received only over-the-counter pain medication and was put in solitary detention, where he remained for more than two months without seeing a specialist or going to a hospital. When Watanabe received an X-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”

Watanabe filed a lawsuit in federal court in Honolulu, alleging that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment by being deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs. He relied on two Supreme Court cases: the court’s 1971 decision in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, holding that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages; and its 1980 decision in Carlson v. Green, in which the court held that the estate of an inmate who died after having an asthma attack could bring a Bivens claim when prison officials had failed to provide adequate medical care for eight hours after the attack and did not send him to the hospital during that time.

The district court dismissed Watanabe’s claim. It held that Carlson did not apply because his claim was not sufficiently similar to the facts of that case.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies to new contexts,” but explained that, in its view, “Watanabe’s claim is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects” and therefore can proceed. A deeply divided court of appeals declined to rehear the case.

Representing Nielsen, Lucas Walker told the justices on Monday that the Supreme Court “has repeatedly explained that Bivens claims are disfavored, that they strain the separation of powers, and that they cannot proceed if there is any reason to think that Congress might be better suited to weigh the costs and benefits of a damages remedy.”

But Watanabe’s “claim ... also fails under a straightforward application of this Court’s Bivens framework,” Walker continued. “There are at least three” “meaningful difference[s] between his case and Carlson.” First, Watanabe had other options besides damages – such as seeking “administrative and injunctive relief.” Second, unlike the inmate in Carlson, Watanabe did not die, which “Congress could see [as] a meaningful difference.” Third and finally, there are “special factors” at play in Watanabe’s case that were not at play in Carlson, such as the Administrative Remedy Program, a grievance process created by the Bureau of Prisons in 1979, and federal laws enacted after the decision, such as the Prison Litigation Reform Act, a 1996 law that requires prisoners to use all available internal prison appeals like the ARP before going to court.

Vivek Suri, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued on behalf of the federal government, told the justices that, in the view of the United States, there are “three ways in which this Court could resolve the case.” “First, it could apply its existing standards and recognize that Carlson is now obsolete. Second, it could ... explicitly overrule Carlson. And, third, it could distinguish Carlson on its facts.” He “respectfully urge[d]” the court to choose one of the first two options, “either of which would abrogate Carlson, fully resolve the” divisions among the courts of appeals “that it has created, and end the severe practical problems that it creates for prison administration.”

Representing Watanabe, Joshua Wesneski reiterated that “the Court’s consistent message for Bivens and Carlson over the past decade” has been “[t]his far and no further.” “‘No further,’ he said, “means we should not extend those precedents. But ‘this far’ means also that Carlson remains settled law within its core context and should not be reduced to a null set. We ask only that the Court adhere to that approach.” “Indeed,” he suggested, “to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress’s measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society’s most vulnerable members.”

Neither Chief Justice John Roberts nor Justice Brett Kavanaugh seemed receptive to Walker’s suggestion that the court should go ahead and overrule both Bivens and Carlson.

Kavanaugh asked Walker how the court should handle the “fact ... that Congress has had 55 years since Bivens and 46 years since Carlson to do so and has not done so?” “It seems,” Kavanaugh continued, “like Congress, in fact, has left Bivens and Carlson where they stood ... and Congress has operated against that backdrop.”

Walker suggested that the Supreme Court “has not hesitated to overrule past decisions, especially those where the courts had overstepped the proper judicial role.”

In response to Walker’s assertion that overruling Bivens would “clear up the confusion and hand the accountability for all of this back to Congress, where it belongs,” Kavanaugh later asked whether “another way to provide clarity [would be] to simply say that courts should apply Bivens and Carlson but not extend them?” He compared such a scenario to what the Supreme Court has done in other areas of the law, such as with the Alien Tort Statute, “where we’ve had results or decisions under a methodology we wouldn’t use anymore, but we have not overruled the original three” causes of action under “the ATS, for example. We just haven’t extended them.”

Suri addressed this point during his time at the lectern, telling Kavanaugh that “[t]he problem ... as I see it ... is the Court’s decision” holding that “the PLRA itself gives rise to a new context,” as does “the availability of injunctive relief.” “So,” he continued, “if you’re going to honor that precedent, then this is a new context,” which would mean that “there are no viable Carlson claims anymore.”

For his part, Roberts noted that the federal government had “expressly” not asked the court to overrule Bivens, “and, of course, they have broad experience in this context. And I wonder,” he asked Walker, “if you have any insight into why or at least why shouldn’t we, on that question, defer to their expertise and experience on that question?”

Walker responded that “I think the answer is that this has been an area wrought with confusion where the lower courts have really called out for guidance.”

Roberts appeared unconvinced. “[O]n the other hand,” he countered, “it could be viewed as a cautious, incremental approach to such a fundamental question” to leave Bivens intact for now.

Several justices focused on whether, if a Carlson claim was not available, an inmate in Watanabe’s shoes would still have some remedy available to him. Justice Neil Gorsuch explored whether an inmate who was the victim of medical malpractice would still be able to obtain relief in a lawsuit against the United States (rather than the individual prison official) under Federal Tort Claims Act, a 1946 law that allows private citizens to sue the federal government for (among other things) injuries caused by a federal employee.

Gorsuch elicited from Suri that “[i]n almost all the cases that” he had “encountered, ... there is an FTCA claim brought in parallel” with the claim under Carlson – in part, Suri suggested, because the standard for prevailing is lower, qualified immunity does not apply, and “[y]ou have a defendant who’s able to pay, the United States.” Suri suggested that when an inmate does not bring both kinds of claims, it may be out of a desire to harass an individual prison official or because the inmates do not have lawyers and are instead representing themselves “and are confused about how to proceed. If this Court says there are no more Carlson claims,” he concluded, “then I think it’s more likely that they will bring FTCA claims in these cases.”

Justice Samuel Alito had a similar question, asking Suri “whether Bivens in this context provides anything ... of value that is not available based on other remedies.”

Suri responded that Carlson had rested on the idea that “the FTCA was insufficient” because it “does not provide for punitive damages.” In Bivens, he emphasized, the court faced a choice between “damages or nothing” for the plaintiff. But under the FTCA, he said, “you’re already getting damages.”

Wesneski pushed back on any suggestion that the FTCA, standing alone, would – as Kavanaugh put it – “provide some remedy in meritorious cases.” The “principal virtue” of the FTCA, he stressed, “is the deterrent effect on the individual officer.” And there would be other potential problems as well, he posited: for example, he said, “we know the plaintiff in Carlson v. Green would not have had a cause of action under the FTCA” under Indiana law.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett also expressed concern about what relief an inmate in a situation like Watanabe’s would be able to obtain. She first pressed Walker on the question of whether an inmate could obtain a court order instructing a prison official to do (or to refrain from doing) something, even if he could not obtain money damages for the official’s past conduct. “I want to make sure,” she said to Walker, “that, in your position, there’s no doubt that someone in a prisoner’s position like this would be able to get injunctive relief against a federal officer.”

And she later returned to a similar topic, asking Walker to “walk me through what happens in a case where a prisoner dies as a result of medical negligence and let’s say really horrific medical negligence. What recourse,” she enquired, “does that prisoner have? Is it the FTCA?”

Walker assured Barrett that, even if Carlson were overruled, claims like the one she described would generally be allowed to go forward.

Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to be the most likely to side with Watanabe. Sotomayor contended that, “in the Westfall Act, Congress looked at Bivens and explicitly reserved those constitutional claims the Court had recognized” – specifically, “Bivens itself for unlawful entry ... without probable cause into private citizens’ homes when there was malfeasance in doing so, and in Carlson itself, which was a ... medical malpractice claim.”

Walker resisted Sotomayor’s characterization, telling Sotomayor that, “respectfully, I don’t think the Court has ever gone so far as to say that the Westfall Act ratified Bivens or Carlson. But what the Court has said is that it does not provide any reason to extend those cases further.”

Jackson seemed to regard Watanabe’s case as, “with respect to all major indicia of sameness,” identical to Carlson. “We have the same kind of alleged violation as in Carlson,” she told Walker. “We have the same constitutional right brought under the same legal framework by the same kind of defendant who’s housed in the same kind of federal institution.”

By contrast, Justice Elena Kagan suggested that, at the very least, Watanabe’s case involves “factual differences.” In addition to the fact that the inmate in Carlson died, she noted that “there was a view that the prison officials had actively contributed to the injury, and ... that the prison officials knew exactly what was happening while it was happening.” “[A] different way of saying the same thing,” she added a few minutes later, “is that this looks like a pretty standard medical malpractice case, bad but standard, where the factual circumstances in Carlson look like something a good deal more than that.”

A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7457. In OpenAI’s Ad Business, Advertisers Come Third

Ads in ChatGPT, it turns out, are a humanitarian effort.

Right at the top of OpenAI’s charter, the company states that its main mission is to bring the benefits of artificial general intelligence (AGI) – meaning AI that can match or outdo people at intellectual tasks – to all of humanity.

“Asterisk, without killing us,” quipped LUMA Partners CEO Terry Kawaja during an on-stage chat with Benji Shomair, OpenAI’s VP of monetization, at LUMA’s Digital Media Summit in New York City on Monday.

But to achieve this lofty goal depends on getting far more people to use ChatGPT than will ever pay for it.

In other words, Shomair said, for OpenAI to fulfill its mission “actually requires [us] to build an ad business.”

“We believe this technology is so beneficial, so incremental, so powerful,” he said, “that we need to create economic means to make it available to everyone.”

But putting ads inside a product that people confide in is a very delicate exercise.

“In my experience, ads or commercial messages haven’t ever been introduced into as intimate an environment as ChatGPT,” Shomair said. “Just think about the things that people are sharing with ChatGPT.”

And so OpenAI is building its ads business around three priorities, in this order: user trust, user value and, last, advertiser value. If you get the first two right, the third will follow, he said.

Which is all well and good as a sentiment. But what do you do when someone asks you to push the boundaries? Which does happen.

Since launching its advertising business less than a year ago, OpenAI has onboarded more than 50 ad tech, measurement and agency partners. “We’re taking a partner-first approach,” Shomair said. “We can’t do it all ourselves; it’s pragmatic.”

Sometimes, however, partners have a different idea of what’s fair game, and OpenAI just won’t go there, Shomair said.

“There are places where I think our partners would like us to do certain things that we just can’t,” he said, “and that’s because of how we think about making decisions.”

OpenAI devised its principles before it even started testing ads internally, and they still shape every product decision, Shomair said.

“We reference these principles on a pretty consistent basis,” he said, “and we use this as a way to communicate to our audiences how we’re thinking about trust.”

Even so, ads in AI chats are an easy punchline. Anthropic’s Super Bowl spots for Claude earlier this year gleefully poked fun at the very idea.

In one, a scrawny guy asks a buff trainer how to get a six-pack fast, in response to which the trainer starts hawking height-boosting insoles. In another, a man asks his therapist for advice on how to communicate better with his mom, and the therapist starts plugging a dating site that connects “sensitive cubs” with “roaring cougars.”

Those Anthropic ads had an impact. Claude’s daily download count went from roughly 63,000 in January to a peak of about 225,000 in mid-February, according to Appfigures, and its daily active users rose 11% after the game, per BNP Paribas.

Shomair acknowledged that the ads were funny. But they don’t reflect OpenAI’s approach to monetization in ChatGPT, he said, where the answers “are separate from the ads and not influenced by the ads.”

Which raises the question of what an ad even is or should be in a product like ChatGPT.

Shomair, who helped build Meta’s ads business before joining OpenAI last December, said part of the fun of his job is that new modes of consumer engagement force him to think about ads differently.

What, for instance, should advertising look like when consumers talk to a brand’s AI agent? Or when their own AI agent does the shopping for them? Or when two agents are just talking to each other?

Shomair said he doesn’t presume to know the answer. Even people working on the bleeding edge, the ones developing these things, are just experimenting, he said.

“It’s hard to forecast beyond six to 12 months,” he said. “The products I was working with 12 months ago versus the products I’m working on now – it’s like night and day.”

But there’s one thing he’s sure of: Nobody should sit on the sidelines. His advice to advertisers: “You’ve got to get your hands dirty,” he said. “You’ve got to jump in and play with it.”

No major retail media player has taken as circumspect an approach to ad revenue as Shopify. But the company has recently taken its next important step with a product called Campaign Autopilot, VP of product for merchant marketing Samir Pradhan tells AdExchanger.

#7454. Shopify Noses Further Into Ad Tech With Campaign Autopilot Expansion

No major retail media player has taken as circumspect an approach to advertising revenue as Shopify.

As the payment processor and site infrastructure for so many online sellers, and with the greatest supply of such first-party data outside of Amazon and Walmart, Shopify holds a unique key for some of the biggest ad platforms.

Initially, the company forged data partnerships with other big platforms so they might target and attribute based on its data – but blindly, with no retargetable ID. Then, Shopify created addressable audience segments and used its data science to create audience segments for other platforms.

In the past quarter, the company has taken its next important step with a product called Campaign Autopilot, Samir Pradhan, Shopify VP of product for merchant marketing, told AdExchanger.

Unsurprisingly, it’s an agentic, AI-driven optimization product. Akin to how other walled garden AI ad products work, merchants set the price they’re willing to pay per sale, including some further controls, such as having a higher incentive for new customers or being able to target by region or time of day.

The current Campaign Autopilot partner platforms are Meta, Microsoft Advertising and Snapchat, with X in the pipeline, Pradhan said. Email marketing and ads on Shop, the Shopify-owned app that aggregates its merchant network, are also available.

And in the past few weeks, the company has added SEO optimization to Campaign Autopilot, he said. “That is our first foray, so to speak, outside of ads toward this broader vision of helping automate more of a merchant marketing.”

(“We don’t currently have the open web,” though. Womp.)

The easy-to-activate advertising solution is important to new merchants, according to Pradhan. Sometimes an ecommerce seller is an expert in one or more channels. But often the entire category is unfamiliar. Small sellers (businesses of one or a few people) aren’t going to hire pro marketers, but they understand the importance of advertising as a core competency.

Campaign Autopilot is a “risk-free ad product,” Pradhan said.

Other big ecommerce marketplaces and retailer or merchant platforms all charge per impression and/or for clicks. They might optimize toward a sale, he said, but it’s not what you actually buy. With Autopilot, though, “Shopify takes that media risk,” he said. The merchant only pays per sale.

There are other guardrails, too, he said. For instance, a campaign can be capped (which sounds commonsensical but has painfully surprised many ecommerce advertisers on other platforms) or an entire channel avoided. And Shopify is working on more “domain-specific controls” (contextual advertising, in other words) for advertisers who want to fine-tune their own campaigns.

Some merchants are sophisticated marketers who’ve honed their own models; others have never spent a dollar on advertising. Pradhan said the idea is to meet a “a broad swath of what marketers try to do from a guardrail perspective.”

Even for veteran ecommerce marketers, though, the industry overhaul to agentic and AI-based ad platforms has happened quickly. For Shopify, he said, “preserving that merchant trust and then making them feel in control was a big part of the ethos of developing this product.”

#7451. When hackers become sources: Inside the new craft of reporting on hacked data

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“You’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.”

Some consequential reporting of recent years has emerged thanks to what is normally defined as a “hack-and-leak,” a specific kind of cyberattack that results in the release of the information obtained by hackers. When Anonymous and allied collectives breached corporations and state agencies during the hacktivist wave of the 2010s, for instance, they turned stolen data into front-page news.

Reporters covering the invasion of Ukraine have frequently worked with documents pulled from Russian institutions by hackers of different allegiances. Hacktivists have breached surveillance vendors and spyware firms, granting journalists direct and exclusive access to the internal files of companies that sell to repressive governments. Ransomware gangs, cybercriminal groups, and state-affiliated hackers deposit fresh troves of hacked data on the open internet, or route it to the public through intermediaries like Distributed Denial of Secrets.

How are journalists responding to these reporting scenarios? For my research, recently published in Journalism Practice, I interviewed 10 journalists across the U.S. and Europe who work or have worked with hacked data. Some of them specialize in the coverage of cyber issues; others mainly focus on current affairs and global conflict. These journalists work for a variety of news outlets, from investigative reporting newsrooms to general interest outlets and technology brands, and have engaged with hacker sources at various levels.

The journalists I spoke with paint a picture of an emerging craft, rather than a settled method. Here’s some of what I found.

There are no fixed guidelines or established and shared practices on how to handle and report on hacked material in news reporting. Instead, the methods are being developed by practitioners on a case by case basis. One reporter who works for an investigative newsroom told me:

Hackers themselves are becoming increasingly strategic about their relationships with the press. One reporter following a specific cyber beat emphasized this:

“I’d say that [hackers] of all kinds love to flex and get credit. A lot of them don’t, but many absolutely do. I’m not sure if the desire to flex has increased, but you’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.

That maturity means developing awareness of how a story will be framed and disseminated and calculating which journalist to approach. Hackers now may select their outlets of choice, matching a leak to the reporter who they think is capable of understanding the story and carrying it further.

There are different kinds of hackers, wearing different and/or multiple hats. Interviewees drew distinctions between financially motivated cybercriminals, whose leaks are often equivalent to extortion by other means, and state-affiliated actors, who may also pose as independent hacktivists to launder politically motivated leaks into credible coverage.

At the same time, some hackers or hacker collectives — like Phineas Fisher, known for his activist remit against surveillance companies — may act for political and public interest–oriented reasons, reaching out to journalists to expose wrongdoing, unethical issues, or crimes. Notoriously, though, hacking is not a field in which hats are worn straightforwardly: Identities, definitions and agendas, including mere trolling, may blur into one another.

Hacked material needs to be handled with a great deal of skepticism. When working with hacked sources, one journalist said, it’s a matter of “treating every dataset as if it has chlamydia.” But the verification techniques the journalists said they use — such as confirming that an email address exists in a company’s records, cross-referencing with known facts, or examining a file for signs of tampering — are fairly conventional. This type of reporting requires more disclosures, especially when a source’s identity can’t be established. One journalist working in this area said:

I think you should be very transparent about that in your reporting. You should say something like, “We don’t know who the source is; it could be the GRU [Russian Federation] or whoever, but we have confirmed that this data is real and this is what it shows.”

Declared openly, the uncertainty may become a meaningful part of the story itself.

Source protection is further complicated when it comes to hackers. Some interviewees extend the full protection they would give any source to hackers, refusing to assist law enforcement even if the source is a self-declared criminal. Others prefer to know as little as possible about their sources, framing the choice as harm reduction for both parties. As one journalist in my sample put it:

The less I know about these things, the harder it’s going to be for me to burn my source or to publish something that inadvertently turns out to be harmful to my source.

Reporters working exclusively with material already circulating online in cybercrime forums or other repositories on the web treat source protection as beside the point, because the origins of the information cannot be traced and because the material is in effect “out there.”

Beneath all of this sits the finding with the widest implications: Ethical decisions in this domain resist strict codification. No general rule can be written in advance, the reporters I spoke with suggested, and judgment in the individual case is the only workable guide. Is publishing hacked material justified? It depends on the specifics of the case at hand, one reporter told me.

I kind of think it all depends on what you’re exposing. Maybe it’s generally wrong to break into people’s computers and steal data, but if you’re exposing serious crimes, then I think it can be justified.

Interviewees described practical wisdom under pressure: the ability to read a specific situation and act appropriately n it, without having the opportunity to refer to an established code or checklist.

Newsrooms, meanwhile, may need to develop verification standards suited to information of illicit origin, transparency norms that treat uncertainty as something to disclose rather than paper over, and a shared language for the ethical judgments that journalists currently make case by case on their own.

#7450. Reddit Taps Qloo To Strengthen Its Predictive Targeting

If someone likes a local Italian restaurant, predicting that they might like another, similar Italian restaurant isn’t exactly rocket science (or, should we say, data science).

What’s a bit more impressive is figuring out that the same person might like a certain fashion brand and have a proclivity for jazz music because they’re looking at a discussion thread about upscale pizza restaurants. Those are the sort of findings that Reddit is hoping to uncover with its new partnership with predictive inference company Qloo (pronounced “clue”).

The partnership, announced on Tuesday, will provide Reddit with access to over 10 years of Qloo’s proprietary data, helping it serve more relevant ads to users.

In 2019, Qloo acquired TasteDive, a multi-industry review and recommendation platform. The data it collects through TasteDive is a key part of its catalogue, Qloo CEO and Founder Alex Elias told AdExchanger. The catalogue tracks correlations between different interests (or “entities”), like restaurants and musical artists, based on shared attributes.

Qloo determines similarities by categorizing entities based on a range of data points from sources, including TasteDive reviews, metadata from the open-source knowledge base Wikidata and data licensed from third parties.

For instance, the famous Italian restaurant in New York I Sodi isn’t just categorized as “Italian food,” Elias said. Rather, Qloo’s knowledge base also pays attention to signals that describe its architecture and ambiance (which Elias described as “Scandinavian minimalism”) so it can be linked to, say, fashion brands with a similar aesthetic – not just comparable Italian restaurants.

Understanding the shared attributes that wouldn’t be obvious at first glance is one of the main reasons Reddit has elected to partner with Qloo, said Virgilio Pigliucci, Reddit’s senior director of engineering.

Users can opt into personalized ads on Reddit, which are particularly helpful when a user is scrolling through their personal feed and engaging with a variety of content, said Pigliucci. But when someone is on a particular subreddit, Reddit generally aims to serve them ads that are “contextually similar” to the posts they’re looking at, he added.

Qloo’s data helps Reddit find connections between products that might not seem to have much in common.

The signals that Reddit gets from its own out-of-the-box data usually suggest advertising a product that is directly related to the post a user is reading, said Pigliucci, like an espresso machine ad on a post about the best coffeemakers.

Using Qloo’s data, Reddit saw that people who are in the market for an espresso machine are also often looking to buy a table that the machine can live on. Now, Reddit might serve an ad for a tall desk on that same thread, rather than echoing recommendations that are already organically cropping up in the conversation.

Historically, it could take days or weeks for Reddit to optimize a new advertiser’s campaign because it needed to track the way users engaged with the ads, Pigliucci said. Now, Reddit has a better understanding of connections between different categories and products and can “optimize against the signals” provided by Qloo by finding a close proxy to the advertiser or ingesting its prior data – no user engagement data necessary.

Plus, Qloo’s data allows for more resonant advertising without requiring any personal data, Pigliucci said. The model draws correlations between entities without having to know the user’s search query, browsing history or even what subreddit they’re in.

#7447. Google, TikTok, and Meta are suing California to stop a law that bans “psychologically exploitative features” for kids under 16

Google, TikTok, and Meta have each filed suit against California in an attempt to block enforcement of a law that protects kids under 16 from “psychologically exploitative features” on social media platforms.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed the law, Assembly Bill 1709, into law this past September. “We want our children–and every California ​kid–to grow up in a world where technology supports their wellbeing, rather than exploits their vulnerabilities,” Newsom said at the time.

AB 1709 prevents socmed platforms from being able to employ features like recommendation algorithms, infinite scroll, and video autoplay on accounts of users under the age of 16. Because of how Google, TikTok, and Meta have designed their platforms, it effectively bans kids under 16 from having accounts at all on YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

According to Reuters, the three big tech companies all said (in separate lawsuits) that California is wrongly forcing them to use a state-mandated method of delivering content to children, instead of leaving things up to parents’ discretion.

Their lawsuits claim violations of Section 230 (aka the “safe harbor” law that lets platforms off the liability hook for anything their users post) and First Amendment free speech protections.

“Parents ‌are best ⁠positioned to make the right decisions for their families,” Google spokesperson Jose Castaneda told Reuters. “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”

Meta’s suit, meanwhile, said California doesn’t have the right to override its editorial standards.

“We are challenging this law because it violates the First Amendment by letting the government dictate how ideas are organized, displayed or shared with Californians,” a Meta spokesperson told Courthouse News. “Under the law, we would be forced to either remove features that keep teens’ experiences age-appropriate, or cut thousands of California teens off from family, friends and their communities.”

TikTok’s suit said ​protected speech “cannot be suppressed solely to ​protect the young from ideas ⁠or images that a legislative body thinks unsuitable.”

“AB 1709 is a blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which book stores, TV networks and streaming services all use,” a TikTok spokesperson added. “Beyond disregarding real progress in making teens safer online, this law limits free speech and takes away parents’ rights to determine what’s appropriate for their kids.”

The defendant in all three suits is California Attorney General Rob Bonta; all three suits ask the court for an injunction that would stop him from enforcing AB 1709 against them.

Bonta’s office said it’s reviewing the suits, and that he is “committed to defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online.”

#7446. Two out of five Americans regularly get their news on Facebook

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Despite what my Facebook feed looks like, the platform’s not just for AI fruit videos and birthday posts.

According to data from the Pew Research Center published Monday, 40% of adults in the United States regularly get their news from Facebook.

That’s up from 36% in 2020, signaling the continued stability of the platform as a news source — a trend that the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism observed in its Digital News Report this year. As we reported in June, people around the world are increasingly abandoning news websites for social media.

The Center surveyed 5,600 U.S. adults in late August as part of its American Trends Panel, and asked respondents several questions about their news and social media habits. Pew did not give respondents a definition of “news,” instead letting them use their own understanding of the term when they filled out the survey. More than half (59%) said that they get news from social media “often or sometimes,” but only 19% actually prefer social media as a place to get news.

Of Facebook news consumers, 33% are men and 49% are between the ages of 30 and 49. The platform is most popular for women (47%), Hispanic Americans (51%), Americans with a high school diploma or less (46%), and Republicans (43%).

Regular news consumption among American users has increased on nine of the 12 social media platforms that Pew studied, including YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, X (Twitter), Reddit, Nextdoor, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. News consumption has either dropped or stayed the same on Rumble, Truth Social, and Bluesky.

The second-most regularly used platform among American adults is YouTube (34%), followed by Instagram (23%), TikTok (20%), and X (10%). YouTube news consumers are more likely to be male (41%), between ages 18 and 29 (39%), and identify as Black (47%) or Asian (53%). Republicans (35%) and Democrats (36%) are equal YouTube news consumers.

The most regularly used platform for news among young adults is Instagram (43%), followed by Facebook (40%), TikTok and YouTube (both 39%), and X and Reddit (both 18%).  The Center found that 20% of U.S. adults now regularly get their news on TikTok, up from 3% in 2020. Of TikTok users, 53% reported getting news regularly on the platform. Nextdoor users are also increasingly turning to the neighborhood forum app for information. In 2026, 45% of Nextdoor users reported regularly getting news from the app, up from 23% in 2022.

#7444. Will AI slop overwhelm creators? Mark Rober isn’t worried–but his team is using AI as a “thought partner” in production

Mark Rober told Business Insider he thinks his content has a “moat” that will keep it safe from being affected by the AI slop deluge.

But, at the same time, he’s said his team is using generative AI as a “thought partner” for writing, and that it can make “the perfect meal” for students using his Class CrunchLabs modules.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

With BI, Rober addressed creators’ anxiety about AI-generated videos encroaching on the watch time that should go to their genuine content.

“Do you want to see a simulation of someone dunking a basketball with a sick trick, or do you want to see someone actually do it?” he told BI. “The fact that [viewers] know it’s real is what makes it crazy.”

He said creators should be reassured that “[o]ur brains developed for hundreds of thousands of years with human connection,” and viewers want “real and authentic” content filmed by people who interact with the world around them.

He also added that people need to retain their cognitive skills instead of just ChatGPTing everything. Both creators and viewers should investigate things themselves, using their own human brains.

“Curiosity is so important in this new age of AI,” he said. “It means you just have a lifetime of learning, versus like, ‘Oh, this thing knows the answer, so who cares?'”

But, again, Rober has implemented AI across his processes. This past June, he told The Information that AI “has the power to really adapt” educational settings.

“Basically what we’re doing with Class CrunchLabs is we’re making great ingredients, really fresh ingredients, and then AI can be like, ‘Hey, I have three kids in my class who are challenged this way, and they’re not great at reading, but these ones are. We’ve already covered this stuff.’ And it could take those ingredients and make the perfect meal for your class,” he explained. “I think it’s gonna be very good at that.”

He said that on the creator side, “I think it would allow me to scale myself in certain ways. We’re certainly using it as a thought partner on writing, on some thumbnail stuff.”

Like he did with BI, Rober said that in science content specifically, viewers probably want something real instead of something LLM’d. “I think it remains to be seen what the public’s appetite is for just pure AI-generated content,” he said. “I would think in science, you actually want to see the lava melt through the thing, versus it just being completely fake. But we’ll see.”

We’ve written before about how big tech platforms like YouTube have found themselves in a tricky catch-22: They want to make money off the AI bubble (uh oh), but as they roll out more generative tools and push creators to use them, they end up combating endless amounts of slop pumped out by those very same tools.

With Rober and other creators, we see something similar: They feel their content is safe from AI content made by other people, but also use AI in their processes, in the name of “scaling” or “ideating” or streamlining and cost-lessening production.

Rober’s team is using AI in its writing process, and a script is the foundation of long-form, educational YouTube content like his. Is the vibe just that viewers won’t care, so long as no fully AI-generated video makes it into an upload? Intriguing…

#7441. The Wall Street Journal’s new AI tool, “Doppler,” forecasts the issues that will shape the midterm elections

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Ahead of Election Day, the tool has ingested 25 million TikTok videos and 500,000 podcasts to gain new insight into U.S. voters.

More than 100 million voters are expected to cast ballots in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

In recent election cycles, political reporting based on voter polling has drawn criticism, prompted scrutiny, and found defenders. As the debate over the value of polling continues, The Wall Street Journal is exploring new ways to cover public opinion and break out of traditional horse race political coverage.

In late September, the Journal published its first story using Doppler News AI, a custom tool built to help expand the publication’s midterms coverage. So far, Doppler has ingested more than 25 million TikTok videos, roughly 500,000 podcast episodes, and thousands of Instagram videos and cable news segments. The Journal uses the tool to monitor trends across the internet and to identify voter priorities, concerns, and sentiments that traditional polling might miss.

RELATED ARTICLEHow The New York Times uses a custom AI tool to track the “manosphere”Andrew DeckFebruary 11, 2026“We’re not trying to predict the election, but people encounter politics through a lot of different lanes: culture, work, money, family, community. We wanted to tap into that and listen in on those conversations,” said Aja Whitaker-Moore, the deputy editor-in-chief of the Journal. “We’re taking a massive set of information…and telling you, from a statistical standpoint: ‘Here’s what people are talking about. Here are the questions they’re asking. Here are the places where those conversations are happening.'”

Other newsrooms have leaned on AI “visibility tools” in the past to support their reporting. That includes using large language models (LLMs) to transcribe and summarize “manosphere” podcasts, school board meetings, and local talk radio shows. But Doppler goes further.

Rather than using AI-generated summaries to generate leads or help beat reporters monitor online content more efficiently, the Journal uses Doppler to conduct large-scale AI analyses quickly — and publishes those insights for readers.

So far, analyses produced by Doppler have led to four major midterms stories in the Journal, with more expected to run before Election Day. For now, each story requires a custom treatment, with engineers and data journalists working alongside the D.C. politics team to refine the methodology, toggle on and off different features, and audit the results.

“The tool is only as good as the questions that you ask it,” said Whitaker-Moore. The Journal holds a weekly editorial meeting leading up to Election Day to workshop story angles and find new threads to explore.

A new in-house AI tool lets WSJ reporters analyze trends in online conversation to help understand the political mood of the country ahead of the midterm elections. A previous post paired a visual of TikToks from across the internet with a headline that identified them as conservative podcasters.

♬ original sound – The Wall Street Journal

A story published on October 8 analyzed over 30,000 hours of podcasts and documented how, in recent weeks, right-leaning podcasters had started discussing “affordability” as often as left-leaning podcasters, despite President Trump calling the affordability crisis a “hoax.”

Another story published on October 1 traced anti-AI sentiment, including opposition to Flock surveillance cameras, by analyzing more than four million TikTok videos and thousands of hours of podcasts. The Journal found that posters who shared anti-Flock sentiments disagreed on other political positions about 12% of the time, three times the average rate across other political topics tracked — putting the issue “at the top of the list of positions that unite creators who are otherwise at odds.”

For a story published on October 15, the Journal pulled content about 67 Democratic politicians from its Doppler database. The analysis showed that the Democratic politician currently receiving the most favorable commentary is Angie Nixon, the progressive Senate nominee in Florida. About 70% of TikTok videos posted about her in recent weeks were favorable. She was followed by Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff at 54%. Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer ranked the lowest in the analysis; just 3% of videos posted about him were favorable.

Whitaker-Moore said the idea for Doppler was inspired by conversations with Washington bureau chief Damian Paletta and politics editor Christopher Matthews. They thought the coverage of the 2024 U.S. election missed important undercurrents in public opinion that never surfaced in polling. And though reporters acknowledged the power of podcasts in that election cycle, there weren’t many standardized ways to capture what was being said across those channels.

Coming out of those conversations, Whitaker-Moore posed a question to Rob Barry, who leads the Journal’s data journalism team: “Can you build something that can eat the internet and then feed it back to us?”

The Journal had already built its own podcast transcription and summarization tool, Orca. (The name refers to the tight-knit pods in which orcas travel.) Orca had collected countless hours of audio and YouTube videos, not just of political podcasts but from genres like health and wellness.

RELATED ARTICLEWhat can The Wall Street Journal’s new ad campaign tell us about its future?Sarah ScireJune 11, 2024The Journal’s experience with TikTok-based investigations made the social media platform’s videos another natural source of information for Doppler. It’s nearly impossible to create a comprehensive database of TikTok videos, or even a truly random sample. Instead, Barry’s team used a monitoring tool that relies on TikTok’s own recommendation algorithms to identify the accounts it should track.

“Every day we’re adding tons of data across all the different platforms that we’re looking at,” Barry told me. “The database is growing in the background constantly.”

To make sense of that data, Doppler has a tech stack that includes different types of AI models, including LLMs. The model used depends on the specific reporting question.

Embedding models have been central to some of stories published so far. These AI models convert text or images into vectors — lists of numbers that capture the meaning of each piece of content. By vectorizing the content, Doppler can map out the ideas in a dataset and see where they naturally cluster together.

The Journal’s data journalism team has used vectorization in the past, including in its Pulitzer Prize–winning story that mapped out Elon Musk’s entire history of tweets. In Doppler, vectorization facilitates a kind of internet radar, helping reporters identify where patterns are forming across its social media and podcasting database.

For now, the Journal’s political reporters can’t just start using Doppler on their own. The exact methodology has been tailored to each story published, with the help of engineers.

RELATED ARTICLELocal newsrooms are using AI to listen in on public meetingsAndrew DeckMarch 13, 2025“There’s a lot of human judgment in this. My team would not have aimed for a tool that seeks to just produce stuff that we then put directly on the internet,” Barry said. “You still need that human intermediary, that human to apply the judgment and to ask the question.”

The Journal is attaching a short methodology to every story assisted by Doppler. It makes clear that AI was used to produce the piece, briefly explains how the analysis came together, and notes some of the tool’s limitations.

Despite manual spot checks of data classifications and other safeguards to make sure the tool’s outputs are accurate, Barry said, “there’s almost always going to be some level of error and uncertainty and blur around the edges.” The disclosures are one way to “give readers a sense for what that level of issue is.”

Looking ahead, the Journal is considering bringing Doppler to other desks in the newsroom. The data being collected is not inherently political, and it could be used to help answer a host of other reporting questions, drawing on insights scattered across the internet.

“We definitely think that [Doppler News AI] can live beyond the midterms and live beyond elections,” Whitaker-Moore said.

#7440. The E.U. wants a new For You Page so that its citizens don’t get stuck in TikTok rabbit holes

Does the European Union have the authority to mandate changes to TikTok‘s For You Page? The continental body is making that claim.

The E.U. announced on Wednesday that the addictive design of the FYP violates the Digital Services Act. A press release discusses the “rabbit hole effect” of TikTok’s infinitely scrolling vertical feed, which is filled with personalized recommendations.

“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” said Henna Virkkunen, the E.U.’s EVP of Tech Sovereignty, Security, and Democracy, in a statement. “The Digital Services Act makes platforms responsible for addressing the negative effects related to their recommender system. Today’s preliminary findings show again that TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ well-being, including those of minors.”

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

The E.U. passed the Digital Services Act in 2022 to give itself a mechanism it can use to regulate the world’s biggest social media companies. The DSA, as the law is known, is particularly focused on negative mental health consequences — including addictive behaviors — that can affect kids when they scroll through their feeds.

E.U. officials cited the DSA when they requested the development of a depersonalized TikTok algorithm, which the app subsequently rolled out. Now, as those leaders set their sights on the FYP, they are making similar requests. One point of contention is the “not interested” icon, which has long been cited as an ineffective form of control for users who don’t want to see specific types of content.

TikTok will get a chance to present documents and plead its case to the E.U. If, however, the app is ultimately found liable for its addictive feed, it could be compelled to pay up to 6% of its annual income in fines.

The validity of that fee structure could provide TikTok with its strongest defense. It previously joined forces with Meta to mount a legal challenge against the enforcement mechanism that undergirds the DSA, and a court ruled in its favor. The attempts to counter the DSA mirror Big Tech’s legal strategies in the United States, where TikTok is one of several companies fighting back against laws that accuse social media feeds of perpetrating psychological ills.

Though TikTok has pushed back against the DSA in the past, the E.U. is not backing down from its threats. TikTok has delivered a major boost to the European economy, but its activity in the region could wind up costing it billions.

#7437. U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The U.K. competition and consumer protection authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss its new commercial terms of service.

On Tuesday, Will Hayter, the executive director for digital markets at the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), shared the update during a session of the communications and digital committee of British Parliament, after a member of the House of Lords pressed him about Meta’s new terms. Hayter said he scheduled a meeting with the tech giant today to seek clarity on the new terms, though the CMA declined to provide any further details.

RELATED ARTICLELegal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesAndrew DeckOctober 17, 2026Last week, Nieman Lab broke the news that the terms would permit mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. The new terms are slated to take effect on October 30, and there is currently no option to opt out. Virtually every news organization owns at least one Meta business account.

“Are you going to pause the deadline? I mean, [it’s in] a week,” Veronica Wadley, Baroness Fleet and a former editor of the Evening Standard, said during the session of Parliament. “You know this includes almost every U.K. news publisher and it is clearly uncompetitive leverage of Meta’s strategic market position.”

In the same session, Sarah Cardell, the CEO of CMA, said the authority had limited intervention options because it has not formally designated Meta as an “entrenched market power” (something it has done in the past for Google and Apple). Cardell said other competition enforcement actions are a possibility, but the CMA is “urgently” seeking more information from Meta before making any judgment.

Over the weekend, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping.

A Meta spokesperson said on Saturday that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service.

“Does Meta think we can’t read?” Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K.’s News Media Association, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Monday. “We know you’ve taken the word ‘train’ out but changing it to ‘develop’ isn’t fooling anyone.”

News publisher associations across Europe have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect next week.

On Tuesday, two major German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review had been conducted. Together, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers represent more than 9,000 media brands across Europe.

RELATED ARTICLEMeet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAIAndrew DeckFebruary 20, 2025“Meta intends to automatically capture, copy, and store the complete websites and archives of publishers and analyze them for its own automated and non-automated commercial products,” reads a joint statement from the associations. “This makes access to Meta’s platforms contingent on the free surrender of the entire digital publishing product. This is blatant theft.”

The statement alleges that Meta’s new terms could be in violation of the E.U. Digital Markets Act, which was passed in 2022 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region. The publishers cited a specific clause that guarantees “fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory general conditions of access for business users.”

The uproar from European publishers echoes similar opposition to the new terms from major U.S. publisher associations. Jason Kint, the CEO of Digital Content Next, has been vocal about his skepticism of the new terms since Nieman Lab’s story broke last week.

“Meta’s supposed Friday night correction to its new commercial terms is a farce,” he wrote in a statement published on Tuesday. “Exactly what you’d expect from a gatekeeper notorious for abusing its market power.”

#7436. UTA, FaZe vets launch ISO as a “new partner for talent”

A new talent firm is launching with a stacked roster of luminaries from the worlds of streaming, social media, and content creation. Mike Lee and Darren Yan are the leaders of ISO, which is kicking off with a roster of 90 top creators.

ISO (the name stands for “in search of”) is a wide-reaching management firm that touch categories like beauty, food, and art, but its roots are deepest in the gaming and streamer communities. Lee, who will serve as ISO’s CEO, was previously the Head of Gaming and Livestreaming at UTA Creators. Yan, ISO’s Head of Music, is the former Chief Talent Officer of FaZe Clan, where he worked to raise up some of the hottest talents on platforms like Twitch.

At ISO, Lee and Yan have assembled a deep roster that includes big names like PlaqueBoyMax, Jasontheween, Ironmouse, Lacy, Vanillamace, Kyedae, jessechrisss, Angelo Marasigan, and RDCWorld. Some of those creators, like PlaqueBoyMax and Lacy, were previously members of FaZe Clan. Others, like Ironmouse and Vanillamace, have history with UTA.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Influence Media Partners is backing ISO as the new firm takes shape. “The next household name is already online, building an audience, and ISO was built for that talent. Today’s gatekeepers are algorithms, so understanding discovery, engagement and how content travels is essential,” Lee said in a statement. “Every creator we work with is running a real business, and our job is to give it room to grow through original IP, products, live events, and expansion into China and platforms like TikTok Shop, where most of the industry still isn’t set up to compete.”

Lee is serious about ISO’s inroads into East Asia. A press release highlighted internation talent like Vietnam’s Son-Tung MTP and China’s Xin Liu, both of whom are part of the ISO equation.

ISO also plans to innovate on the brand-facing side of its business. Its core team has experience at companies like the NFL, Red Bull, and Fanatics, which are on board as talent partners. Matt Alsberg, ISO’s Head of Talent, previously held roles at PlayStation and Twitch.

With a wealth of ideas and an abundance of talent up and down its roster, ISO is ready to become a management company with deep knowledge of the creator ecosystem. The creators working with ISO are known for their brash, bold-faced personalities — and that attitude seems to fit the firm to a tee.

#7433. Have you heard? Ethan and Hila’s divorce, Harvard’s creator summit, and Brandon Herrera’s defeat.

Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

This week, infidelity is bringing an end to a high-profile creator marriage, the Ivy League is hosting a new kind of summit, and we’re still waiting for the first creator in Congress.

Hila Klein files for divorce as Ethan’s affair becomes public. The Kleins were well known as co-hosts of a podcast and YouTube channel, but Ethan is being removed from his positions after his indiscretions came to light. And that’s not all — Hila wasted no time filing for divorce. She had already made that decision before the news became public, and she will seek joint custody of the couple’s kids while also restoring her maiden name.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Sour Patch Kids owner sues Ryan Trahan over candy brand Joyride. Consumer goods giant Mondelez is arguing that Trahan’s candies were designed to be confused with Sour Patch Kids, because they’re human-shaped and wrapped in colorful packaging. The actual case might be complicated, but this is yet another roadblock for a creator-led consumable product.

Alex Cooper heads to CAA after UTA exit. The Call Her Daddy host will look to turn over a new leaf as she brings a new talent firm into her corner. CAA is choosing to represent Cooper, her husband Matt Kaplan, and their media company Unwell, so the L.A.-based agency is making a big bet on a major Gen Z tastemaker.

Harvard University’s School of Public Health hosted a creator summit. More than a dozen creators were in attendance as Harvard looked to improve the quality of health information of social media. Platforms like TikTok are increasingly popular as sources of medical advice for Gen Z users, so the summit is an important step in the right direction as healthcare professionals look to counteract the spread of misinformation.

YouTube is bringing a Grand Theft Auto “creator collective” to London. On October 17, two days before the arrival of the much-anticipated next chapter in Rockstar Games’ open world franchise, YouTube will gather gamers and creators in West London for an event that will celebrate the launch of GTA VI. The game is expected to be the biggest gaming tentpole of the year, so it’s no surprise to see platforms pulling out all the stops to generate excitement.

Can Paris Creator Week become the Cannes of the creator economy? That question was on everyone’s mind as 8,000 attendees flocked to the French capital for two days of typical convention fare. All of the major social media players were represented, as were European content producers like Banijay. All of a sudden, France has become a major hotbed for creator events.

Firearms YouTuber Brandon Herrera lost his Congressional bid. Running for a House seat in a deep-red district, Herrera was favored to become the first Congressman whose career began on social media. But the blue wave that crashed down in Texas swept Herrera aside, as Democrat Katy Padilla Stout earned a comfortable victory that will send Herrera back to YouTube.

TikTok edits might not be the right choice for political ads. That was one takeaway from a recent study that examined the social media messaging of Kamala Harris’ 2024 presidential run. The researchers concluded that traditional ads work better on social media than posts that try to adopt those platforms’ stylistic conventions. Translation: Promote your campaign on TikTok, but keep it simple, stupid.

Jubilee follows up election stream with short-form push. The media company delivered its first election special on the night of the 2026 midterms, and days later, it announced its first two short-form originals. Dateable and People Spotting will help Jubilee break into new territory as it builds on its reputation as a wide-reaching content producer aimed at Gen Z.

The financials of Instagram’s move into long-form content are drawing questions. Creators want to buy into Instagram’s plan for 90-minute videos, but without a robust revenue stream attached, some are skeptical. “Exposure as a form of payment and with the intention of cutting into YouTube’s market share and cutting into the amount of views people are getting on YouTube — it’s just gross,” digital strategist and creator Gabriella Zutrau told Digiday. “Instagram has never valued creators.”

YouTube’s app redesign has proven to be perplexing. The new version of the YouTube app moves the Subscriptions tab to a menu that goes away once the user starts scrolling through their feed. YouTube redesigns are always unpopular at first, but the platform’s repeated minimizations of its famous subscriptions is definitely a curious choice.

Snapchat’s subscription offerings now have 30 million customers. As Snap Inc. revealed its earnings for the third quarter of 2026, it touted the continued success of products like Snapchat+ and Lens+. By offering premium features in exchange for a cost-effective monthly price, subscriptions have become a key part of Snap’s business model and monetization suite.

Why watch YouTube when you can build your own in two hours. That’s what Andrej Karpathy did with a little help from a fellow named Claude. The result of that effort is HackerTube, which contains thousands of videos related to the titular subject and shows what can be accomplished with AI-assisted coding.

Why is ‘Sacrifice’ the first Elton John music video with one billion YouTube views? ‘Sacrifice’ is a 1989 single that peaked at #18 on the charts, but it gave John his first entry in the Billion Views Club. You would think that ‘Tiny Dancer,’ ‘Your Song,’ or ‘Benny and the Jets’ would have broken through first, but it’s going to be a long, long time before those singles can match ‘Sacrifice’ on YouTube.

Humanoid robots put to work at a China supermarket are “slacking off.” Why bust your circuits when you can just quiet quit like all those humans who programmed you? The bots’ questionable work ethic is just smart — that’s why they call it artificial intelligence.
