#7389. Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Grokipedia shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

When I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia said “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”

I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

That article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D.

Still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds new content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It shows that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. Grok’s voracious internet searches sometimes find things that human editors don’t. The long article about me includes a substantive discussion of my research about lying in politics and my work with fact-checkers around the world, neither of which are in the Wikipedia version. Grokipedia also provides some welcome balance. When it offers context, Grokipedia can be a little heavy with hype (“His work has been lauded for innovating transparency in media…”) But it also included a “Criticisms and Controversies” section that details complaints that PolitiFact is biased against Republicans. That section has a healthy back and forth about the critiques and my response. That kind of balance could be helpful for Wikipedia, which has taken heat from Musk and others for being too lefty. Musk’s encyclopedia also has a playful spirit that Wikipedia could learn from. Grokipedia’s homepage features random samples of recent edits that provide a glimpse at how the site is being improved. Another Grokipedia feature reads articles aloud in an AI voice you select: Eve, who sounds like a BBC anchor; Ara, a serious woman with crisp diction; Leo, who might have been a professor at Oxford; and Sal, whose name suggests a sports bar but whose voice is NPR. My big takeaway from Grok is the importance of human judgment in curating knowledge. Grok is a bot trying to behave like a human editor. Its many mistakes and lousy writing show that AI is not ready to replace Wikipedia’s talented volunteers. Still, Grok shows that AI can be a tool that helps them research and write better articles. After seeing an AI encyclopedia up close through my experiences with Grok, I come away with hope. Yes, AI can be a sloppy researcher and an awful writer. But Grok’s performance, shaky as it was, highlighted AI’s readiness for higher-level responsibilities. Bill Adair, the Knight Professor of the Practice of Journalism and Public Policy at Duke University, is writing a book about how Wikipedia editors are adapting to the age of AI.

Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he said was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet.

With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a new version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.”

When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had big aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video.

For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia shows edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make.

Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk.

Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. The 25-year-old encyclopedia has long been a source and beneficiary of Google searches. Wikipedia provides the answers and in turn benefits from readers clicking through to read articles. But when people make a query to a chatbot, they often get the answer they need in an AI summary and don’t click through to read the encyclopedia article. That threatens donations because fewer readers see Wikipedia’s fundraising pitches. Wikipedia has banned content generated by LLMs, but that hasn’t stopped many contributors — some well-intentioned, some not — from dumping an avalanche of AI-written content on the site. That has put a huge burden on the site’s “New pages patrol,” the editors who approve articles, because they must weed out the lousy content. (Wikipedia has a helpful guide of LLMs’ favorite words and phrases, such as “tapestry” and “meticulously” and sentences that start with “additionally.”) Still, terrible as it is, Grokipedia offers lessons in how AI can help Wikipedia. #7388. Ziff Davis CEO: ‘Not Planning On A Search Recovery’ via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

A large publisher says organic Google referrals fell again and pointed to Search Console's AI report. Here's what its AI impressions comparison measures.

Ziff Davis says organic Google referrals to its properties fell about 37% year over year in the third quarter. CEO Vivek Shah told analysts on the company’s Nov. 6 earnings call that referrals fell about 23% in the same quarter last year, putting the two-year decline at more than 50%.

Shah referenced an impressions figure from Google Search Console as well. Ziff Davis’ digital media sites generated about 2.7 billion impressions for both AI Overviews and AI Mode during the quarter, which was nearly 10 times “the clicks those same sites received from Google Search” based on his estimates. Other sites that have Search Console’s generative AI report are able to generate the same comparison. Google’s definitions show this compares impression counts inside their AI feature reporting vs. all click throughs from Search.

Shah said Ziff Davis is “not planning on a search recovery” and expects referrals to keep falling. Third-quarter revenue fell 5.6% to $289.3 million, a smaller drop he attributed to businesses that don’t rely on Google traffic, such as subscriptions and apps.

Shah said an impression is a count of “how many times a link to a page was shown inside generative AI features” and that this figure is coming from Search Console. Google has a help page to explain what the generative AI performance report does and it says the report counts the number of times links to a site appeared in AI Overviews and AI Mode. Since the report draws these two features from the Web search data within the main Performance report, AI impressions are a subset of a website’s total Search impression figures.

Google’s help page on how clicks are counted says a click on a link to another website within an AI Overview or in AI Mode counts towards a site’s total click count. None of the Search appearance types listed by Google for the Performance report includes either feature.

Shah did not say during the call where he got his click total from. If Shah used Search Console to get his total clicks from Google Search, then those clicks would include AI Overview clicks, AI Mode clicks and every other possible type of result in Search. This means that Shah’s ratio is comparing AI feature impressions to all clicks from Search. As of Nov. 8, Google documents no separate AI click count.

I covered how Search Console counts AI clicks last week, after Google’s Gary Illyes said the company had nothing to announce yet on adding more data.

Shah referred to “the disruption of search traffic by Google and LLMs” as a clear business headwind. He said that Ziff Davis’ tech and shopping brands “continue to face the strongest search traffic headwinds in our portfolio”; however, he also highlighted offset areas, such as social commerce and the relaunched RetailMeNot app.

Ziff Davis’ tech and shopping revenue declined 3.8% year over year during the quarter to $82 million (as reported in its earnings presentation). The decline has narrowed for three consecutive quarters per Shah’s account.

Shah said Ziff Davis’ largest property based on search referrals, IGN, has continued to hold up relatively well. He explained that “a lot of its search referral is around game help, which is very maps heavy” and that it is difficult to duplicate game maps. IGN also receives a significant amount of direct traffic.

Despite that, gaming and entertainment revenue declined 2.1%, and Shah attributed the decline to the poor gaming advertising environment leading up to the release of Grand Theft Auto VI later this month. He added that IGN’s business is significantly driven by video, including vertical and social video, versus web traffic.

In his comments to investors during the Ziff Davis earnings call in November 2025, Shah said AI Overviews were present in 29% of search queries that generate the majority of Ziff Davis’ traffic. While there had been a slight decrease in the percentage of searches containing AI Overviews, he was more concerned with overall Google search volatility than with AI Overviews themselves. His current figure for that quarter’s referral decline is about 23%.

In August, he said AI Overviews appeared on about 50% of the queries relevant to Ziff Davis’ properties, up from about 36% when he last gave the figure. He didn’t give an AI Overview share on the Nov. 6 call.

Shah said making money from Ziff Davis’ content in AI answers was “the priority”, and that they are open to licensing agreements. Additionally, he expects the pending litigation by Ziff Davis against OpenAI will help clarify this space. In his words, “there is a gap between usage and monetization” even as marketers give more weight to AI visibility when choosing media partners.

Ziff Davis plans for referrals to continue declining; Shah’s method will provide each of these sites that have the generative AI report with a large publisher’s number to place next to its own. Those sites can recreate the ratio by comparing their AI impression data to their web search click data for the same time period. Since clicks on AI link results are included with all other Search clicks, the result cannot be used as an AI click-through rate.

The UK’s Competition and Markets Authority has set a Dec. 3 deadline for Google to give publishers impressions, clicks and click-through rate for AI search features in the UK, aggregated across features such as AI Overviews and AI Mode, according to the regulator’s summary. As I reported last week, the CMA’s interpretive notes name Search Console as one example of where that data could appear.

Watch how Google provides those metrics around Dec. 3. If it reports AI clicks apart from other Search clicks, publishers could line them up with their AI impressions.

#7385. Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft will make it easier for publishers to opt out of being scraped

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”

Anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI says it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an important step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

AI search now runs on two internets. Build the organic stack that gets your brand cited on both, prioritizing pages, communities, video & reviews.

Your rankings are holding. Your clicks aren’t.

Google’s AI features answer the question on the results page, and the searcher never leaves. From January to April 2026, 68% of U.S. Google searches ended without a click. And less of Google’s traffic reaches the open web than it used to.

Because for a growing share of B2B buyers, the search doesn’t start on Google at all. It starts in an AI chatbot.

Google’s results page, its AI features, and the standalone LLMs all pull from a mix of sources. Reddit threads. YouTube videos. Review profiles. LinkedIn posts. Comparison pages.

That’s your organic growth stack. It’s also the mix your buyers use to build a shortlist.

If you only optimize your site, you’re competing for a shrinking slice of the pool. To stay competitive, SEO has to expand beyond on-site.

Today, I’ll show you which sources each surface leans on and what to build first.

For our State of B2B AI Discovery 2026 report with AirOps, we tracked roughly 380,000 AI answers covering 81 enterprise software topics across six AI surfaces. Unless linked otherwise, the figures below come from this study.

Let’s start with what didn’t change. Product pages still get cited more than anything else.

Across every AI surface we tracked, vendor sites, integrators, and tool directories took the largest share of citations. That ranged from 52% on Perplexity to 72% on Gemini. Review sites added another 9% to 21%.

Remember: Vendor share isn’t yours by default. It includes your competitors’ sites and the software directories that list you side-by-side.

This is the stack’s foundation, and it’s crowded. Your product pages compete with your rivals’ pages. The comparison pages written about you compete with the ones you write yourself.

The layers above the foundation are where search starts to splinter.

Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode ground their answers in live Google Search results. They inherit what already ranks. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity run their own retrieval.

The citations split right along that line.

Google’s two AI surfaces put 7% of their citations into social platforms like YouTube and LinkedIn. ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude sit at 0.3% or below.

So “AI visibility” is at least two games.

A brand can be everywhere in Google’s AI answers but invisible in ChatGPT and the other standalone models. Or the reverse. Using a blended visibility score hides each one’s contribution.

See also: Wikipedia, Podcasts & Reddit Now Drive AI Citations, Ask Your PR Team How They Did It

Organic visibility now comes down to surface coverage: showing up on the domains each AI surface trusts most.

Your new organic growth stack has to address both internets. Here’s how to do it.

See also: What Search Engines Trust Now: Authority, Freshness & First-Party Signals

AI tools are catching on fast with B2B buyers. According to G2, 51% of B2B software buyers now start their research in an AI chatbot more often than Google, up from 29% a year earlier.

But Google still dominates search overall. It handles roughly three-quarters of all desktop searches. AI Overviews alone reach 2.5 billion monthly users and another billion use AI Mode.

I still think ranking matters. It just doesn’t guarantee a citation anymore. AI Overviews have been pulling fewer citations from top-ranking pages.

The standalone engines lean on product pages too.

Gemini sends 72% of its citations to vendor and product domains, while G2 shows up in just 14% of its answers. Gemini is choosing between vendor pages, and yours are up against everyone else’s in your category.

Eighty-four of the 100 most-cited URLs in our data were either comparison pages (59) or listicles (25). Together, they drew over 66,000 citations. Whoever writes those pages shapes how AI frames your category.

A lot of teams pour budget into the blog and let product and comparison pages go stale. I’d flip that. Fix the pages AI already cites before you write another post.

As James Scherer, Foundation’s VP of Strategy, puts it: “Editorial gets the budget; product pages get the citations.”

Action: Identify the 10 most-cited comparison pages and listicles in your category. Check how you’re framed in each one. Then publish your own comparison page against your top three competitors.

Reddit was the most-cited external domain in our dataset, earning 159,000 citations across 12,500 unique URLs.

Reddit’s logged-out users, who mostly arrive from search engines, grew 27% year over year in Q2 2026. They now outnumber logged-in users, 77.7 million to 52.6 million. Threads rank on Google. Google sends readers into the threads. Then Google’s AI features cite them.

But those layers can also shift fast. After reports that ChatGPT was citing Reddit less, we extended our tracking and found its Reddit citation rate fell from 21% in July to 10% in August, while Google’s surfaces kept citing Reddit.

How much community platforms like Reddit matter also depends on your category. Community citations ranged from 5% of the total for SEO platforms to 14% for EDR/XDR security tools.

If you’re new to the platform, start with this SEJ AMA with a Reddit marketing veteran.

My biggest advice: Don’t treat Reddit like a launch channel. I’d trade one viral thread for steady, useful answers across 50.

Action: Spread your effort across many threads and subreddits. Don’t bet on one. Track community citations weekly, because monthly reporting would have missed a drop like ChatGPT’s.

LinkedIn is a Google-surface play. It reaches 13% of AI Mode answers, 9% of AI Overviews, and 6% of Perplexity’s. ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude didn’t cite it at all.

Across B2B software categories, social is the second-largest citation source after brand and product content, at 6%.

LinkedIn is where executives and practitioners set the category narrative. Google’s AI features pick up that narrative. It’s why employee amplification belongs in the stack.

Don’t fall into the likes and follows trap. If the goal is getting cited, watch whether Google’s AI answers pick up the way your people describe the category.

Action: Pick the category questions you want to own. Post on them every week from executives and practitioners. Measure the impact in AI Overviews and AI Mode, since that’s where LinkedIn gets cited.

YouTube shows up in 47% of AI Mode’s citing answers and 38% of AI Overviews.

It’s tempting to read that as Google favoring its own property, but our data complicates that. Gemini is also a Google product, and yet YouTube showed up in 0.3% of its citations: roughly 17x less than on AI Overviews.

The difference is how each surface finds its sources. AI Overviews and AI Mode are Search features. Google uses query fan-out, running multiple related searches to build each answer, so videos that already rank in Search get pulled in.

A lot of B2B videos are made for people who already know your brand and product. But the videos that earn a place in this layer answer the questions buyers ask before they’ve picked a vendor.

Action: Ship comparison, alternatives, and best-of videos. Title them the way your buyers phrase the question.

The standalone engines lean hard on review sites. Claude and Perplexity draw about one in five citations from review domains.

Claude’s third-party citations are almost entirely review platforms. G2 appears in 30% of the Claude answers that cite sources. Capterra appears in 13%, and Gartner and PeerSpot in about 9% each.

Category matters here too. Review citations ranged from 8% in managed databases to 25% in ATS and recruiting software.

Buyers back this up. In G2’s 2026 research, review sites (38%) narrowly passed AI chatbots (37%) as the top source shaping B2B software shortlists.

G2 isn’t a one-time push. For Claude and Perplexity, your profile is a live source, so run it like one.

Action: Give your G2 profile a named owner and a monthly review target.

Nobody builds every layer at once. Run two checks before you start.

Copy the wrong organic growth stack, and you end up investing in the wrong channels. The AirOps data shows just how much the source mix changes from industry to industry, even within the SaaS space.

The managed database niche is an illustrative example. A brand in this space that borrows an HR tech playbook pours budget into review sites, which earn just 8% of that category’s citations. Meanwhile, it starves communities, which earn 13%.

Once you know which layers matter in your category, match them to the team you have. At every size, the question is the same: which internet are you still missing?

Run a fixed set of 100+ prompts on a schedule. Track citation rate and share for each AI surface. Set an alert for any 20% week-over-week swing.

Watch sentiment per platform, too. On the same prompts, AirOps’ 100-point sentiment scores ranged from 81 on Perplexity to 69 on Claude.

Then tie it back to the numbers leadership already watches, like branded searches, referral traffic, and pipeline sourced from your content.

The first quarter is slow. You’re fixing old comparison pages and setting baselines nobody asked for.

By month 12, it compounds. Your comparison pages are the ones AI quotes in your category. Your review profiles stay fresh without a scramble. Your threads and videos show up when Google answers your buyers’ questions. And when a platform changes what it cites, you catch it that week.

Last month, you built the engine. Now you know where to point it.

Search gets you found. The stack gets you chosen.

#7381. Why An AI Usage Report Stopped Comparing AI With Search Engines via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

An updated AI usage report says it can no longer reliably compare AI used for search with search engines. AI referrals grew but stay a small share of traffic.

Graphite’s updated AI usage report puts six AI assistants at 76 billion sessions a month worldwide in September, up 37% from a year earlier. Unlike the agency’s March edition, it doesn’t compare that usage with search engines.

In March, the agency put monthly AI sessions at 56% the size of search worldwide and 34% in the U.S., with search-related AI use at 28% and 17%. The new report says that edition likely undercounted Google search use from Google’s Android app, and that the agency “can no longer reliably compare” the size of AI used for search with search engines.

The session counts are Similarweb estimates of web visits plus mobile app sessions. The report doesn’t include desktop apps because, as it explains, there isn’t reliable data available for them. Graphite sells SEO and AEO services, while Similarweb sells the data.

According to the March report, search engine usage was calculated based on website visits only (not including the apps), since the apps saw little use.

However, according to the November report, the Google Android app is different, accounting for an estimated 11.8 billion monthly sessions in the U.S. People use the app for image recognition, translation and Google Discover as well as general search. The agency says it has “no reliable data source” to determine what percent of these sessions are related to general search.

The March report’s 56% figure for total AI session usage used a web-based only count of search engines. In addition, the March report’s estimate that ChatGPT accounted for 20% of global search-related traffic used the same count. Although the new report does not revisit either of these numbers, as of this writing, the March page is still highlighting these numbers as some of the major findings from that report, though there is a link to the new report at the top.

The report’s data “suggest that AI accounts for less than 1% of traffic on average” to websites. A separate chart of U.S. traffic in the second quarter of 2026 puts organic search at 49 times the volume of AI referrals and paid search at eight times.

AI referral traffic has grown from that small base, up 92% year over year worldwide as of July and 75% in the U.S. The report’s referral figures cover the top 43,000 sites among domains with at least 100,000 monthly U.S. visits in six or more months between July 2023 and July 2026. It tracks AI referrals to those sites worldwide and in the U.S.

In July, ChatGPT accounted for 60% of AI referral traffic worldwide, followed by Gemini at 14% and Claude at 10%. In the U.S., ChatGPT’s share was 66%, while Claude accounted for 11% and Gemini for 10%.

Between July and December 2025, global session activity with the six assistants increased by 2.3%. The report describes this as a plateau. Then global activity with all the assistants rose by 19% from January through September 2026.

Year-over-year growth in U.S. session activity was 45% in September.

Worldwide session activity with ChatGPT grew 24% year over year. ChatGPT also represented 58.9% of the sessions added.

Claude had the largest increase (in percent) globally, at 1,901%. Claude also generated 26% of the additional sessions. Perplexity was the only assistant among the six to show a decline, falling 27% globally.

Most global sessions occurred on mobile (mobile app or mobile web), at 89% in the third quarter of 2026. Mobile comprised 78% of sessions in the United States.

Graphite’s data for Google in March was only from measuring the number of visits to Google’s website. The agency now says it can’t determine what percentage of the total usage of the Android app is search. OpenAI didn’t include the actual Google figure when it said that ChatGPT receives approximately one-fifth as many search-like queries as Google. I wrote about this on Nov. 3. The two estimates also count different things, with OpenAI logging a search whenever a question sends ChatGPT to the web and Graphite counting website visits and app sessions.

Before an AI-to-search ratio goes into a channel plan, check how its source counted Google.

Graphite cites anecdotal evidence that some visits prompted by AI answers get credited to direct visits or branded search, which AI referral reports wouldn’t catch. Its early numbers suggest branded search traffic is fairly flat year over year, with full results to come.

That measure is broader than the one in Similarweb’s June data, which I covered. Among people who visited a brand’s site after ChatGPT recommended it, 55.9% of that traffic came through branded search, in U.S. desktop data.

#7378. Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”

Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

“Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”

Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

To reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

“The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”

Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”

CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

“We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”

Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”

Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.)

Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. Only 21% were “doom only.”

The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

“We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”

What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.)

“I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”

Part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”

#7377. SEO Split Testing In 2027: How To Prove A Change Actually Worked

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Before & after charts don't prove SEO results. Here's how to run an SEO split test, read the numbers and report a result your CFO will trust.

A client asked us a question recently that I wish every client asked.

We sent over a few ideas for their product pages, and one came back with a note: “If we ran this as an A/B split test, what metric would we measure it on? What are we actually trying to achieve?”

It’s a fair challenge. It’s also the one SEO has historically been the worst at answering.

For years, the standard answer has been a before-and-after chart. We changed the title tags in March, clicks went up in April, and everyone nodded. But anyone who has presented SEO results to the C-suite knows the follow-up: “How do you know that wasn’t just Google?”

In 2026, that question is harder to dodge than ever. Core updates, seasonality, and AI Overviews can all move your traffic without you touching a thing.

I’ve written this article from the agency side of the table, where proving a result is part of the job. I’ll be covering what proof actually looks like, how an SEO split test works, which method fits the site you have, and how to report a result so it survives the boardroom.

A before-and-after comparison tells you that something changed. It can’t tell you what.

Organic traffic to any group of pages is being pushed around by a lot of things at once:

Then there’s the results page itself. AI Overviews and AI Mode can change how often people click without your ranking moving at all, and Google counts that AI feature data in the overall Search Console performance report.

So the real question isn’t “did traffic go up?” It’s “did traffic go up more than it would have without the change?” That estimate is called the counterfactual, and every credible SEO test is really just a way of building one.

See also: How Do I Know If AI Overviews Are Taking Clicks From My Site And What Can I Do About It? – Ask An SEO

In my experience, a result that holds up in front of a finance team almost always has four things behind it:

That last point is exactly what our client’s question was getting at. If you choose the metric and what counts as a win after you’ve seen the data, you’ll always find a way to call it a win.

It also forces you to decide what the change is actually for. A title tag rewrite should move clicks from search. A layout change designed to help shoppers compare options is really a conversion test first, with search metrics as a guardrail.

The fix is a short brief, written, and shared before anything goes live:

It rarely needs more than a page, and it changes the final conversation from “do we believe you?” to “did it pass the test we agreed on?”

Giulia Panozzo’s recent piece on the mistakes that undermine SEO experiments goes deeper on the design side.

SEO split testing often gets confused with CRO testing, which splits users between two versions of a page. That doesn’t work for SEO.

Google only ranks one version of each URL at a time, so splitting users can’t tell you how a change affects rankings or clicks from search. And showing Googlebot different pages from the ones people see is cloaking, which Google’s guidance on website testing says is against its spam policies “whether you’re running a test or not.”

So an SEO split test splits pages instead of people. You take a group of pages built on the same template, like product, category, or location pages, and divide them into two buckets. The variant pages get the change, and the control pages stay exactly as they are.

Matched buckets. The two groups need to behave the same way before the test starts. Keep pages that compete for the same queries together as one unit, or a winning variant can simply take clicks from its control twin.

Then match units by traffic level and category and randomly assign them. Some platforms automate the balancing, like SearchPilot’s smart bucketing.

A concurrent run. Both groups run over the same dates, so a core update or a holiday spike lands on both at the same time. That doesn’t guarantee they’ll react the same way, since an update can hit some categories harder than others. That’s why the matching and the check below matter.

A forecast. The control group is used to model what the variant pages would have done without the change. The gap between that forecast and what actually happened is your result.

A pre-launch check. Pick a few pretend launch dates in the past, train the model on the data before each one, and see how well it predicts the weeks after, using windows the same length as your test. If it keeps “finding” effects in periods where nothing happened, it won’t be able to tell you what your change did.

Google’s open-source CausalImpact package is the best-known model for building that forecast. SearchPilot started out on it before moving to a neural network model in 2019 so it could pick up smaller uplifts.

Not every site can run a textbook split test. SearchPilot’s rule of thumb is that the section you’re testing should get around 1,000 organic visits per day.

Below that, tests tend to drag on or never reach a clear answer. That doesn’t mean smaller sites can’t test. It means choosing the right design and being honest about how strong the evidence is.

If you’re limited to a pre/post comparison, you can still make it far more defensible:

The tooling follows the same split. Enterprise platforms like SearchPilot and seoClarity’s SEO & AEO Split Tester handle deployment and modeling, SEOTesting.com runs Search Console-based tests for smaller sites, and CausalImpact is free if you have data support in-house. If your CMS already lets you change a subset of pages on a template, you may not need a platform for your first few tests.

A good SEO split test report only needs a handful of numbers.

Uplift against the forecast. The difference between what the variant pages did and what the model expected. It’s your headline, but it should never appear on its own.

The interval. The range of effects the model considers plausible. Bayesian tools call it a credible interval and others a confidence interval, but either way, if it includes zero, the result doesn’t show a positive effect.

Probability of a positive effect. This is the easiest number for non-technical stakeholders to follow, but check what your tool is reporting. CausalImpact’s “probability of a causal effect” doesn’t say which direction, so a confident loss can score as high as a win.

Be careful with framing, too. A 90% probability of a positive effect still leaves a one in ten chance the change did nothing or made things worse.

Revenue or conversions on the tested pages. The number that turns an SEO result into a business case. Revenue is noisier than clicks, so treat it as directional if volumes are small.

Rankings can help explain why clicks moved, but compare them against the control group too. They’re never proof on their own.

See also: Reporting Uncertainty Without Losing Credibility

Google says Search Console’s Search Generative AI performance reports rolled out to all sites on Aug. 31, 2026, although sites with too few AI impressions won’t see one. The reports show how often your pages appeared in AI Overviews and AI Mode, broken down by page.

So you can compare AI feature impressions for your variant and control groups, the same way you would click. If a change lifts clicks but loses AI visibility, or the other way around, that’s worth digging into before you roll out.

There’s no click data yet, so treat it as a supporting signal. And if you’re using rankings as supporting evidence, remember that every link in an AI Overview is given the position of the AI Overview itself, as Google’s John Mueller recently confirmed.

Here’s what a clean test looks like from start to finish. The numbers are illustrative, but this is the shape you want before you face a CFO.

The change. A new title tag and meta description template for product pages, rewritten to lead with what the shopper is searching for instead of the brand name.

The brief. The primary metric is non-branded organic clicks, and conversion rate can’t fall more than 2% relative to control. The smallest lift worth acting on is 5%, and the analysis date is six weeks after launch. The template rolls out only if the 95% interval sits entirely above zero, the central estimate clears 5%, and the guardrail holds.

The split. 400 product pages, clustered so pages competing for the same queries stay together, then matched by traffic level and category and randomly assigned. That gives roughly 200 variant and 200 control pages, and the setup passes the pre-launch check.

The result. At six weeks, variant pages get 14.2% more non-branded organic clicks than the forecast built from the control group, with a 95% credible interval of 8% to 19%. The model puts the probability of a positive effect at over 99%, and the conversion data rules out a drop beyond the 2% guardrail.

The interval first clears zero on day 27. The test still runs to the agreed six-week mark, and the effect holds.

The business outcome. Organic revenue from sessions landing on the variant pages comes in 9.6% above its own forecast. Its interval is much wider than the click result, so it’s reported as directional. Average position on target terms moves from 6.4 to 4.8 while the control group holds steady, which helps explain where the extra clicks came from.

The decision. The template rolls out to the remaining product pages. From then on, you’re monitoring that the gain persists, since there’s no longer a control group to prove it.

Most tests won’t look this tidy. In 2024, SearchPilot re-ran what it called a representative sample of past tests through its newest model, and 29% came back positive at 95% confidence, up from 13% with its previous best model.

So even with a purpose-built model, most of those tests didn’t show a significant win. That doesn’t mean the changes did nothing, but it’s worth knowing before you push something sitewide.

Lead with the decision, not the methodology. Most stakeholders want to know three things: what you’re recommending, how sure you are, and what it’s worth.

A one-page report that covers this usually looks like:

The recommendation: Roll out, roll back, or record it as inconclusive.

The result in one sentence: “Our model estimates the new template lifted non-branded clicks to the tested product pages by between 8% and 19%.”

What it’s worth: Revenue or leads on the tested pages, plus a rollout projection with its assumptions spelled out.

How you tested it: The pages, split, dates, and method, plus anything that happened during the test, like a core update.

For the projection, start from the conservative end of the range, spell out how the remaining pages differ from the tested ones and call it a scenario, not a result. If the full rollout beats a conservative number, you build trust. If it misses an optimistic one, you lose it.

And report the losers. A test log that only contains wins looks like cherry-picking, because it is. Sharing negative and inconclusive results is what makes the wins believable.

Monitor daily to catch implementation problems, but make the call on the planned analysis date, unless your platform uses a method built for continuous monitoring. Calling a test the first time it crosses the line makes it much more likely you’ll roll out a false positive.

Some tools apply changes with JavaScript. Use the URL Inspection tool to confirm the change appears in the rendered HTML, and check the variant pages have been recrawled since it went live.

For title tests, also check what Google is actually showing. Google rewrites title links when it thinks it has a better option, so the title you’re testing isn’t always the one searchers see.

The client who asked what metric we’d measure wasn’t being difficult. They were holding SEO to the same standard as every other channel in their budget.

Split testing won’t make every change a winner. Plenty won’t be. What it does is replace “trust us” with a result your stakeholders can check for themselves.

Write the brief before you start, compare against a fair control, report a range instead of a single number, and tie it back to revenue. Do that consistently, and “how do you know that wasn’t just Google?” becomes a question you can actually answer.

#7373. The Onion’s new plan to market its print newspaper: sponsoring a bowl game

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.)

On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:

The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM

For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one company or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.)

Collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently said no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.)

So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The New Orleans Bowl.

I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM

Then the folks who run the New Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM

Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in New Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and said it straight up: "No."

We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM

While the New Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

#7371. Google Ads Tests A Weekly AI Report Card For Your Ad Creative via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Some Google Ads accounts show an Asset activity page that uses AI to deliver weekly insight cards on ad creative, including headline ideas to test.

Some Google Ads accounts are showing a beta page called Asset activity, which gives advertisers weekly insight cards about their ad creative.

Google Ads practitioner Anthony Higman posted a screenshot on LinkedIn on Nov. 6, calling it an AI feature he likes, and asked whether everyone had it. In his screenshot, the cards suggest new headline themes, point to top-performing headlines and report an increase in searches for legal consultation guidance. The only reply to his post, as of Nov. 9, said no.

When I checked on Nov. 9, I couldn’t find any mention of Asset activity on either Google Ads Help or the Google Ads announcements page.

Asset activity is located in the Assets section of the Google Ads menu (between the Assets report and Videos) and has a Beta label.

The insight cards on the page carry a weekly update label. Each card includes a category, date range, headline and View details link, plus feedback options.

In Higman’s screenshot, the cards can be filtered by four different categories, named Featured, Asset performance, Asset diversity and Industry trends.

His Asset diversity card is titled “Add financial recovery headlines to attract injured riders” and is marked Oct. 21-27. His Asset performance card is titled “Higher clickthrough rate for top-rated headlines” and contains a section entitled Top-performing headlines.

His Industry trends card reports that the number of search queries related to seeking legal consultation guidance has increased. It recommends creating headlines with simple consultation details.

Between his cards and the Weekly activity panel is a message saying that this tool uses artificial intelligence and could be providing users with inaccurate information. The panel shows that the most current week is Oct. 19-25. Because the screenshot ends there, it doesn’t show what data is reported by the panel.

Google Ads already tracks asset performance and updates in many areas.

Google has a help section (Performance Max asset reporting), which says that the Assets report will allow you to compare performance by asset, asset group or one or more campaigns. The Last updated field provides the date for when an asset was last changed (added, modified, paused or removed).

Search trends on the Insights page provide categories related to your business that have shown large increases in searches from one period to the next.

Ask Advisor (Gemini-based advisor within Google Ads) is also in beta; it takes asset audit requests and provides examples of what you can ask about like “How am I performing against my peers?”

Asset activity collects insights about specific headlines on one page and refreshes them each week.

The first metric listed on the Asset performance card in Higman’s screenshot is click-through rate (CTR). Google lists CTR, CPC, CPA and ROAS at the asset level as “directional indicators only” because assets are shown together. This guidance applies to Google’s existing asset reports, and the screenshot does not show how these new cards determine their findings.

You should use a CTR-based card as a starting point to test a headline and then review the results at the asset group or campaign level, which are the levels where Google suggests you evaluate performance. Before keeping a headline suggested by the Asset diversity or Industry trends cards, check how it converts in your own account.

As of Nov. 9, there was no help page or announcement about which accounts or campaign types receive the Asset activity page in Google Ads. Google has yet to explain how these cards are created.

Look for a Beta-labeled Asset activity entry in the Assets section of your accounts. Watch for a page on Google Ads Help that explains who receives this new page and how the cards are generated.

#7368. With “Bimbo University,” Nikita Redkar leans into femininity to explain the news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

“I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

For Nikita Redkar, a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

“I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”

Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent.

Tameez: Tell me about why this work is important to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved. When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like.

It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved.

Tameez: Tell me more about that. You have a little bit of an online persona. Redkar: That was the whole reason I created Bimbo University. I wanted to get more women on board with being interested in politics and history in particular, because history is seen as such a male-dominated [field]. It was really important to me to bring, colloquially speaking, the girls and the gays and the theys into the space, because it is fascinating and it provides context to what we’re going through right now. It makes the present a little less daunting when you study historical cycles and realize that people 100 years ago dealt with [similar things to what we’re going through now]. How did they come out of that?

Tameez: How do you define your niche and how did you get there? Redkar: My niche is educational. Bimbo University is a place where anyone can start no matter where they are [in their political education]. My audience [ranges from] people who are just getting into politics to people who maybe were triggered by a specific event in the news to start paying more attention to it. I feel like leftist content creators all operate on a spectrum. You have people who are getting really deep into Marxist theory, for example, and things like geopolitics. I’m at the beginning. I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, “OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.”

Tameez: You’re the first news creator I’ve talked to who does Get Ready With Me videos. You take all of your interests and apply them [to your videos] to be relatable. Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.” That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that. But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.
