#7330. “F*** Keywords” – Well, What Are You Replacing Them With? via @sejournal, @chrisgreenseo

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Declaring keywords dead is easy. Explaining what you’ll track, how you’ll govern content, and what stakeholders buy into is the harder part.

Every so often, someone in SEO announces “f*** keywords” or a similar sentiment. It’s not really a “hot take.” Moreover, it’s something that we see time and again.

Sometimes it’s a fair reaction to how reluctant some people in the industry are to change. Other times it feels more like a meme response, or a flex. A way to show you’ve moved on from old-school SEO without saying much about what you do differently, exaggerating a tension between pro/anti keywords without understanding it.

I have some sympathy for the sentiment for sure. I’ve worked on too many campaigns where success came down to whether a handful of keywords went up or down. Once those rankings became THE GOAL, it was easy to spend more time explaining two dropped places than asking whether we met the primary business need. More damagingly, in the worst cases we were left making decisions just for promoting keywords, rather than the business goals they were supposed to enable.

I don’t know how many people still run campaigns that way, and I suspect fewer than the “f*** keywords” cry implies. What interests me is how quickly the argument goes from “this is a bad way to judge a campaign” to “why are we thinking about keywords at all?”

Take an example search like [hotels near Heathrow with a shuttle]. It’s a decent shorthand for what someone wants to know before they book. Is there a shuttle to the terminal? Does it run when my flight lands? Do I need to reserve a seat? It also gives you a clue about what language you need to use to gain recognition from the searcher.

If guests are looking for a shuttle, the page titled “ground transportation solutions” is making them do more work than they need to. Again, a fictitious example, but I have lost track of how many times in my career I’ve seen businesses wanting to target the ways they define their products/services, NOT how people search for them.

In this instance, what is more important is that the initial search query becomes emblematic of a series of questions that need answering, potentially across a series of pages. Whether we call this a hub and spoke model, or a content cluster, whatever, we have captured part of the customer journey with a query and then determined the potential related queries.

This is where a keyword map (or site map) earns its keep, long after the initial research is done and the content written and published. Imagine that six months later someone rewrites a particular location page. The shuttle timetable moves into a general FAQ and a new transfers page goes live. All three changes are totally logical, but taken together, they can leave the site without a clear place to answer the question the location page used to own. Without realizing it, you have sleepwalked into undoing the research you have done before.

If you’ve recorded which page serves that need, the next content editor or SEO has something to go back to. They can ensure that intent/search query is still considered, move content responsibility, update the internal links, and ensure the redirects are done. The keyword map preserves the reasoning behind those original decisions and helps you tell the difference between an intentional change and targeting that drifted over a few rounds of perfectly reasonable edits.

The keywords aren’t the single truth, nor are they to be treated as an immutable dogma, but throwing them in the “f***it bucket” could be missing something important.

Too cool for keywords now? Great, but how does governance work? How do you ensure you’re not wasting the money already spent on research? Yeah, I know – that sounds tedious, because it can be. And building a process to make sure this isn’t painfully manual IS hard.

You can organize your work around topics, and you can use embeddings to help group the language – in fact you should! But at some point, you’ll at least need to benchmark overall visibility, and you still have to choose what to type into a search box or put in a prompt. You can aggregate your rank/prompt tracking for a content cluster – which is needed – but before the aggregation comes selections of individual prompts and terms.

Stakeholders need to buy into those prompts/terms/queries that make up that group OR you 10x the number of specific tracked elements to totally de-emphasize any individual one. Not a bad idea, but you increase your costs significantly and still need to consider the wording, terms and intents on individual pages when it comes to making optimizations.

Instead, I’d happily track a few representative searches for a given page, where I would also want to see which URL(s) appeared and whether they answered the question. Those observations can tell us whether the page is doing some of the work we intended, whether another page is potentially conflicting and where our own content is falling behind competitors.

“Wait, we still use keywords in our data, but we don’t report on the success of individual keywords anymore!” That is perfectly sensible, but it turns out that maybe, perhaps, the “f*** keywords” position is more clickbait than actual smart thinking – right?

These are SEO basics; I totally understand. Prompt tracking and AI search do ultimately de-emphasize the importance of exact keywords in favor of meaning. But consider that embedding text into vectors is so “machines” can understand it. Your team, colleagues and stakeholders still need the human version to understand how to optimize and tell the story of what is/isn’t working.

All of this helps us understand what we’re visible for, but it doesn’t tell us what happened next – and that is perhaps the biggest weakness.

In Search City, I wrote about the temptation to only optimize for the bits of the search journey we can see. Rankings were always one of the easier bits to observe – that is why we have had an almighty job replacing them with a more useful metric, and why the issues hitting prompt trackers are so disruptive to the industry! But now, even when someone makes a search and sees you for that query/keyword/prompt, the part that links that moment to a click and then an important business event can be almost totally disconnected.

Knowing whether we “rank” for a keyword or not is still an important data point. Fixating on that single data point is mad – but that goes for any single data point. We need to use it to build the picture, build a story and provide insight.

If I went back to any of those campaigns I ran where I felt single terms were prioritized (to a fault), I’d probably still keep some of the same keywords – as triggering as that may be.

I’d use them to agree which searches mattered the most, decide which pages should serve them and check whether those pages still do the job. When it came time to judge the campaign, I’d want to know what happened to the customers/clicks we were trying to win. That was the question the rankings were supposed to help us answer in the first place, and it is still something they can help answer today.

This post was originally published on Chris Green SEO.

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to 10+ countries in English and launching multiturn ads in the U.S. Here is what PPC advertisers need to know about reporting.

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to more than 10 new countries in English while launching multiturn ads for follow-up queries in the U.S.

Google shared the update from its official Google Ads X account on November 9, following an earlier LinkedIn post from Dan Taylor noting plans to bring ads in AI Mode to additional countries in Q4.

Eligible campaigns can already participate, though advertisers still can’t see AI Mode performance separately in Google Ads.

Here’s what’s changing, how conversational placements work, and what you need to know when clients ask about AI Mode reporting.

Google’s October announcement named 10 additional countries where ads in AI Mode are expanding:

The expansion currently supports English. Google also announced plans to bring ads in AI Mode to Brazil, Mexico, and the United Kingdom in Q4 2026. Those markets were listed as upcoming rather than part of the initial rollout.

Google’s availability documentation notes that Pakistan supports text ads only.

Multiturn ads are launching in the U.S., allowing ads to appear on follow-up questions within an AI Mode conversation. Google hasn’t announced when those placements will expand outside the U.S.

Google describes AI Mode as a search experience for questions involving exploration, reasoning, or complex comparisons. Users can ask a detailed question an dcontinue with follow-ups as they work through their options.

AI Mode may use “query fan-out,” issuing related searches across subtopics and data sources to develop a response.

With multiturn ads, Google can show an ad during those follow-up exchanges when the conversation has commercial relevance.

According to Google’s advertiser documentation, ads can match directly to a search query or draw on context from both the question and AI response. An exploratory question can then create an advertising opportunity even when the user hasn’t searched for a specific product.

In his LinkedIn update, Taylor noted that people are asking longer, more detailed, and exploratory questions in AI Mode, and described many of those interactions as upper-funnel queries that carry commercial intent.

For advertisers, that means ads may reach people still comparing approaches or deciding what they need. A longer question or another follow-up does not, on its own, indicate that someone is ready to buy.

As ads in AI Mode expand, clients will likely ask whether their campaigns are appearing there and how those ads perform.

In my view, the most important thing for agency and in-house teams to communicate right now is that reporting is limited, and you can’t separate out AI Mode performance granularly.

Google’s reporting documentation confirms that AI Mode impressions, clicks, conversions, and costs are included in standard campaign reporting. Search terms are also combined with other traffic, without a separate AI Mode breakdown. That prevents advertisers from calculating an AI Mode-specific CPA or ROAS.

Google’s keyword prioritization documentation also says reported search terms for experiences including AI Mode may approximate the user’s intent. Advertisers should not assume they are seeing the exact question someone entered.

Teams can still review those terms for relevance, compare conversion performance, and check lead quality. If results change after the rollout, though, the timing alone can’t directly establish that AI Mode caused it.

When clients ask how AI Mode ads are performing, advertisers can explain that those results are included in campaign totals. Google Ads doesn’t report them separately, so teams can’t show how much spend or how many conversions came from AI Mode.

Google is adding countries and follow-up placements without giving advertisers a separate view of their results.

That leaves teams answering questions about AI Mode with campaign-level data. A campaign could improve overall while AI Mode underperforms, or the reverse, and the combined totals wouldn’t show that granularity.

Separate reporting would help advertisers understand which searches and placements are producing sales or qualified leads. Until Google provides it, teams can explain how their campaigns qualify for AI Mode, but can’t necessarily tell clients what those placements contributed to.

#7323. McDonald’s US CMO steps down as sales decline

As the fast-food giant searches for a new marketing leader, it will split the role between two longtime executives on an interim basis.

Alyssa Buetikofer, chief marketing and customer experience officer of McDonald’s USA, will leave the company next month to spend more time with her family, according to an internal note obtained by Marketing Dive. A 15-year veteran at McDonald’s, the executive was appointed to her latest role less than two years ago when Tariq Hassan stepped down.

As the company conducts a search for its new U.S. CMO, its marketing will be supported by two current executives in interim roles. Global CMO and Head of New Business Ventures Morgan Flatley will also serve as interim chief creative officer, while company veteran Charlie Newberger will serve as interim senior vice president, U.S. chief marketing and commercial officer.

The shakeup arrives a day after McDonald’s reported that U.S. comparable sales declined 0.2% in Q3 2026. However, global comparable sales increased 1.5% and the company beat Wall Street expectations.

Buetikofer will remain with McDonald’s through Dec. 18 to help support the leadership transition. The note cited her impact on McDonald’s business, where she recently oversaw the return of Snack Wraps and Monopoly, as well as the launch of a new beverage platform and a successful Grinch collaboration.

Flatley previously served as U.S. chief marketing and digital customer experience officer from 2017 to 2021 before taking on the global leadership role. She is described in the note as the driving force behind the brand’s “Fan Truths” strategy and the “Famous Orders” platform.

“In today’s environment, creativity is the difference maker for brands, and Morgan’s leadership puts us in a strong position to develop big ideas that build the brand and accelerate growth,” according to the note.

Newberger has been at McDonald’s for more than 17 years and was most recently corporate vice president and global category head for beverages and desserts. In the interim, he will lead marketing operations and work to translate strategy into commercial execution across the U.S. business.

The leadership moves and CMO search come as McDonald’s works to implement a strategic plan that it unveiled in June and detailed at a September investor day. Marketing is part of a consumer-focused pillar of the plan that includes creating brand-led content and co-creating with fans to reach consumers in relevant and personalized ways. McDonald’s last month also stepped away from the FIFA World Cup, a move that could disrupt the QSR sports sponsorship space.

Google's latest core update is rolling out worldwide in all languages. The company calls it a regular update, and rankings may move during the rollout.

Google began rolling out the November 2026 core update today, according to the Google Search Status Dashboard. The rollout started at 10:06 a.m. PT. Google says the update applies globally and to all languages and may take up to two weeks to complete.

The company’s Search Central account also announced the update on LinkedIn. It’s the third Search core update this year. Google recommends waiting until the rollout is complete before checking your Search Console data.

Google’s Search Status Dashboard entry reads:

“Released the November 2026 core update, which applies globally and to all languages. The rollout may take up to 2 weeks to complete.”

“This is a regular update designed to better surface relevant, satisfying content for searchers from all types of sites.”

The exact wording in that sentence is what Google used for its March core update.

As of posting time, no specific objectives are mentioned on either the dashboard entry or the LinkedIn post. The Search Central blog doesn’t have a post regarding the update either. Google’s core updates page carries a revision date of Dec. 10, 2025.

The May core update finished rolling out on June 2, more than five months before today’s launch. Three spam updates ran in between.

The November update is the eighth ranking update listed on the Search Status Dashboard so far this year.

Some sites may experience rank changes during the rollout of the November core update. Google’s core updates document advises waiting at least a full week after the completion of a core update, then comparing your Search Console data from that week to a week prior to the start of the rollout. Google’s suggested baseline in advance of the November update is a week prior to Nov. 10.

A full two-week rollout would finish around Nov. 24. The week immediately following Nov. 24 will include U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Retail sites looking at this time period compared to a pre-update week would be looking at holiday traffic against a regular week.

According to Google, core updates don’t target specific sites or individual pages and are meant to keep its systems current as content on the web changes.

Per its LinkedIn post, Google will update its ranking release history page once the rollout is complete. We’ll update this article then, too.

#7318. Campaign Trail: Wet Ones puts ‘hand butts’ on the streets

The Edgewell brand worked with BBH USA on an out-of-home campaign it hoped would cause some consumers to do a double take.

It’s cold and flu season, which means it's prime time for consumers to reach for antibacterial hand wipes. And while Wet Ones has been keeping hands clean consistently over the last half century, the Edgewell Personal Care brand had not released a major campaign in years.

Wet Ones decided to change that, seeking to create something fresh, bold and different that could capture the attention of a younger audience. The brand teamed with BBH USA and kept the brief loose: get the brand back out there and in conversations. The result, “Just For Hands,” launched last month and grew from a simple insight: More than 50% of consumers have used hand wipes on an intimate area, according to research commissioned by the brand.

“It was a bit surprising to us because it wasn't something that we had necessarily seen before,” said Nicole Harris, head of marketing for sun and skin at Edgewell. “We can do something with this. This is funny. How can we play on this?”

The insight about how consumers were using hand wipes inspired early rounds of work that played off inanimate objects like peaches. But BBH kept pushing and landed on an idea that the team calls “hand butts:” extreme close-ups of fingers that look like posteriors.

“We wanted to create a double take – that split second when you think you're seeing one thing, and then realize you're looking at something completely different,” said Yohan Daver, executive creative director at BBH USA.

“The craft had to make the illusion feel completely real, and by taking the idea across New York City at scale, we're turning one clever visual device into a much bigger cultural moment,” Daver added.

Created with photographer Ale Burset, a winner of more than 60 Cannes Lions awards, the campaign had a comprehensive out-of-home media plan including LinkNYC kiosks, transit shelters, digital newsstands, wild postings, bus wrapping and a Time Square takeover. Plus, interactive walls dispensed travel packs and individual wipes to pedestrians.

Originally, Wet Ones’ media plan included ads throughout the New York City subway system, where the variety of handheld surfaces like railings and straps provide a “torture test” for the product, Harris explained. That changed when the Metropolitan Transportation Authority vetoed the “Just For Hands” creative.

“When they refused us for being a little too risque, it was perfect,” Harris said. “It added juiciness to the story, but it also forced us to think quickly in terms of the other touch points. How do we want to evolve the media plan to still have the impact, but also take advantage of this from a storytelling perspective?”

Wet Ones’ PR team used the rejection as an angle to drive earned media. The brand also partnered with Kyle Cooke, of reality TV series “Summer House,” for a social stunt that brought a hand butt to celebrity gossip account DeuxMoi. Then, the “Just For Hands” campaign became the target of some friendly banter from Goodwipes, a brand of flushable wipes — not hand wipes — that isn’t a Wet Ones competitor.

“We [wanted] to get a response up in Times Square, so that was probably a record that I've seen, in my tenure for the company, for us to turn around a piece of creative and get it up within hours,” Harris said. That type of speed and agility was central to the “Just For Hands” campaign.

“We kicked it off at the end of August, so really fast turn out of the gate, but [it] led to amazing work,” Harris said. “We're getting great consumer response, but our retailers were really excited about it, too.”

You'll be embedded within Service Operations, and your primary job is to make every engineering team more reliable — not by owning their infrastructure, but by establishing the practices, frameworks, and feedback loops that let them own reliability themselves. Act as the reliability expert teams pull in for architecture reviews, failure mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design

Identify and quantify operational toil across the org, and build or advocate for automation that eliminates it

Meta removed ‘train’ from its crawl clause, kept ‘develop’, then paused everything. The pushback worked once. Do not expect it to work twice.

Meta backed down this time. On Nov. 5, it paused new business terms that would have let it crawl the website of every business using Facebook or Instagram, after publishers, a court, and a regulator pushed back. Pushback can work. But a business that gets its customers through Meta should plan as if Meta will never get better for it.

In October 2026, Meta previewed new business terms, the rules a business accepts when it uses Facebook or Instagram for business: a Page, ads, a shop. The first version let Meta use automated software to read the websites tied to a business, to “provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain” its products. Accepting was the price of staying, and the only way to say no was to stop using Meta for business.

On Oct. 16, Meta took the word “train” out and limited the crawl to its advertising and business products. “Develop” stayed in, and so did the crawl. On Oct. 23, Meta moved the start date from Oct. 30 to Nov. 20.

Meta doesn’t say why it paused. Paused is not withdrawn. Nieman Lab reports Meta’s notice says “our existing terms remain in effect”, and nothing in it says what comes back, or when.

Meta has done things that work for Meta since forever, with no regard for anyone. This is what Meta does. Hollywood has made two films about Facebook, and neither is about how well it treats its users.

Meta’s pattern feels like a slow death for a business in the Meta ecosystem, with nothing it can do about what Meta changes. Reaching for a business’s website is new. The attitude isn’t new: Meta not caring about its business users, and trying to give them no options.

So start investing in other acquisition channels, or at least planning for them.

Meta backed down this time. Do not wait for it to do it again.

This post was originally published on No Hacks.

#7313. How Lands’ End’s holiday pop-up feeds an always-on marketing strategy

Sarah Sylvester, who joined the retailer as CMO in March, digs into how a Holiday Tree Farm experience helps meet other imperatives.

Lands’ End is coming home for the holidays this year with an immersive pop-up in Chicago, the city where the Wisconsin-based lifestyle retailer was founded in 1963. The Holiday Tree Farm by Lands’ End is inspired by a line of archival copy that said that the retailer of apparel, outerwear and home furnishings provided “everything but the tree” at Christmastime.

“I just loved what that evoked, as far as being able to sum up how Lands’ End can help you for your holidays, because we literally have something for everybody… I feel like that really embodied what we were trying to accomplish,” CMO Sarah Sylvester said. “Lands’ End has done events in the past for holiday — how can you not? — but we really wanted to make sure that we were challenging everyone to think outside of the box.”

The holiday effort arrives as Lands’ End continues its turnaround efforts. The retailer and brand management firm WHP Global in April completed the creation of a joint venture that is intended to help those efforts. Lands’ End saw net revenue increase 2.7% year over year in Q2 2026 and made moves on marketing spend, customer acquisition and inventory that executives believe will better position it for the back half of the year.

The Holiday Tree Farm, open Nov. 6-8, will feature a variety of seasonally themed experiences, including a tote bag customization station, a vintage photo booth and a cozy lounge. The pop-up’s stations connect with the retailer’s key seasonal product categories — like outerwear and pajamas — so that the experience remains grounded in the brand.

The activation also includes a Holiday Drink Lodge in partnership with coffee chain La Colombe and a Sweater Swap in partnership with resale platform ThredUp that allows guests to exchange a used sweater for a new one.

Lands’ End’s prior collaborations with convenience store chain Wawa and lifestyle brand T&T Twin Talk were cited on a recent earnings call as marketing highlights that helped drive social media traffic and retail sales. But brand collaborations need more than just shared marketer interest, according to Sylvester.

“Even if you have really great brand names, if it doesn't make sense in some way, shape, or form with audience overlap or shared intent, it's hard to make it work,” the executive said. “We want to always ground it back to key product categories, either for us or them… how do you cut through the noise and do something that's fun and disruptive?”

Beyond other brands, Lands’ End is also partnering with Chicago native Lindi Presta and her Running the Runway run club for a “Miles & Monograms” activation and hosting a book reading and signing with local children’s author Lori Orlinsky. The goal of collaborating with such influencers is to help Lands’ End foster stronger local ties and extend the experience beyond Chicago.

“With these types of events, yes, you want to get broad awareness and great social content… even if you can't physically be at the pop-up in Chicago, you can still see and appreciate the content and enjoy it,” Sylvester said. “But specifically with Chicago, I love the localization aspect and how we're really trying to connect with the community.”

Lands’ End’s holiday pop-up arrives at a moment when marketers are reembracing experiential marketing after pandemic disruptions and amid a pendulum swing away from pay-to-play performance marketing toward IRL brand building. The retailer earlier this year teamed with Graduate by Hilton for a “Tote Tailgate Tour” that featured onsite experiences at three college towns.

“I started my career in experiential, so it holds a soft spot in my heart,” Sylvester said. “More than ever, people are craving things in real life and real experiences that they can participate in… There's just something nostalgic and comforting about when you can put down your phone and interact in real life. I think events and experiences are more important than ever.”

For Sylvester, who was appointed in March as Lands’ End’s first chief marketing officer in nearly a decade, experiential is a part of the brand’s always-on marketing — not just an opportunity for a few social posts and possibly PR-driven articles. That approach comes as some marketers are using experiential to help meet other needs around content creation and discoverability in the age of artificial intelligence.

“Experiences cost more than just paying for another paid social ad — how do we make that investment go as far as possible? Yes, it's about, hopefully, the thousands of people that will physically come through and interact with us, but also about creating content for holiday that we can use all season long,” the executive said.

In an increasingly fragmented consumer environment, uniting all aspects of the marketing mix — paid media, paid social, search, influencers, brand collaborations and experiences — around one core brand story is crucial, Sylvester explained.

“I feel like you need these three or four big moments a year of really being clear about who you are and what you stand for,” she said. “In marketing, you’ve got to do a little bit of all of it. It's always an ‘and.’”

#7307. 5 social signals brands should act on now

Social media leaders are expected to know what is happening everywhere, all the time, and to have a point of view on what to do about it. But most social tools were built to monitor and measure. They report what happened. They rarely explain what it means.

That gap is where real opportunity sits. Across the brands we analyze each week, the most useful findings are rarely the biggest numbers. More often they are the shifts underneath them.

Here are five that marketing teams should be paying attention to.

Audiences are tiring of hyper-polished, solo "it-girl" glamour and gravitating toward content that feels like friends in a room. A candid carousel recapping a New York Fashion Week party reached nearly 740,000 accounts and drew more than 21,000 engagements, outperforming standard step-and-repeat coverage.

The action: Retire the solo interview. Try conversations and group chats where co-hosts or friends interview each other. Lightly produced and unscripted. Shift production focus from rigid scripts to creating environments that foster authentic interpersonal dynamics and natural conversational flow.

For one consumer tech brand, the most powerful emotional anchor was not a feature. It was relief from small, familiar anxieties: a dying battery, a package that might arrive while you are offline. Humorous, relatable posts about those moments drove strong reach and shares on Instagram and Facebook.

The action: Build bite-sized, highly visual scenarios that show the product solving an everyday problem. Focusing messaging on specific, common friction points rather than broad feature lists quickly builds emotional resonance and everyday relevance with your audience.

Many brands treat Stories as a place to repost the grid. But more often, short form content, like Instagram Stories, acts as a high-intent conversion powerhouse, generating massive click-through rates that can surpass follower reach.

The action: Rather than treating Stories as a secondary syndication feed, start treating them as optimized, high-velocity checkout funnels. Consider story-only offers and unique promo codes that turn intent into sales you can attribute, and design ephemeral content tailored for rapid action with clear, direct calls-to-action.

Relatable humor and conversational copywriting significantly outperform traditional feature-benefit structures in driving post engagement and click-through actions. We’re seeing meme-style copy ("My package: out for delivery / Me: I'm gonna be offline...") consistently outperforming feature-and-benefit announcements.

The action: Write the first three seconds of a Reel the way people actually post, using script-style overlays, familiar phrasing and emoji cues. Adopt native platform vernacular and visual formats to capture scroll attention and increase viewer retention.

Communities are starting to exhibit strong skepticism around highly marketed aesthetic features. For one technology brand, this was showing up in cases where customers felt basics were unaddressed: camera quality, software availability, stability. Sentiment scores alone would have missed the credibility gap.

The action: Show features in real-world moments where they are useful, not in isolated product shots. Frame product capabilities within everyday consumer workflows or challenges to demonstrate tangible value and maintain brand credibility.

Manscaped, the men's grooming brand, built a following by being very good at one kind of humor. But as the brand looked to expand into face and beard care, it needed to adapt its comedic approach to resonate beyond its below-the-waist roots.

Rather than doubling down, the team used cultural AI to find its voice by watching audience signals and how they responded to new creative. That surfaced new creator partners, including two University of Southern California student filmmakers who helped create one of the brand’s most viral pieces of content to date. It also helped validate the creative concept behind the brand's fall 2025 "Send Face Pics Instead" campaign, which contributed to Manscaped’s broader efforts to expand its reach and become the #3 brand in the U.S. Total Electric Shave Market.

All because cultural AI delivered rapid insights in a form leadership could confidently act on. The brand’s social director described it as "a quick postcard brief to make your point on why we need to act on something and to get the social teams heard."

None of these signals required more data. They required context: what is changing, why people are responding and what to do next. That’s what happens when you stop tracking the signals and start reading the room.

#7305. Reddit highlights opportunities for financial services marketers

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company released TransUnion data suggesting that financial promotions in its app outperform similar campaigns on other platforms.

Reddit is making a pitch to financial marketers by highlighting data that shows how effective financial services ads are in the app.

This is probably not the first market sector that comes to mind when considering Reddit’s promotional potential for ads. But with more than 500 million weekly users, Reddit has a large audience of people exploring all kinds of topics.

As explained by Reddit: “Reddit brings together people actively seeking answers with communities built around shared experiences and expertise. For Financial Services shoppers, those conversations can play an important role in the decision journey. 62% of financial services shoppers in the UK on Reddit say that reading honest, unfiltered experiences from everyday people is an important factor when researching products or services, and 70% in Germany say Reddit helps them buy with confidence.”

In order to highlight the value of the app for financial services promotions, Reddit commissioned TransUnion to conduct a marketing mix modeling analysis of the in-app financial promotions that have run in the region comprising Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The study showed that financial services advertisers are seeing 9 times returns on their Reddit ad spend, which the analysis said is much higher than this sector sees in other apps.

A key benefit of Reddit ads in this context is that the promotions can amplify the impact of financial services ads across other platforms.“TransUnion found that 81% of Reddit’s total impact came directly from Reddit, while 19% came from improved performance in other channels — nearly one-fifth of its impact showed up elsewhere on the media plan,” Reddit said.

The data showed that paid search drives the biggest benefit in this respect.

That makes sense, given that Reddit posts have increasingly been cited by search engines and artificial intelligence chatbot responses. As such, increasing discussion around a brand in the app would have expanded exposure potential.

However, it’s also worth noting that Reddit has seen a major decline in search referrals lately. The platform reported last week in its Q3 earnings that search referral traffic dropped by more than one million referrals on average per week in October.

That would likely reduce the expanded benefit of Reddit exposure through promotions.

Either way, Reddit could offer expanded opportunities to reach interested consumers seeking financial services info and products.

#7301. How Ogilvy uses AI to unlock scale, protect rights for brand talent shoots

The WPP agency launched Echo in collaboration with Creative Artists Agency to meet marketers’ content needs while preserving consumer trust.

Ogilvy on Monday announced the launch of Echo, a proprietary artificial intelligence platform that allows advertisers to generate additional assets from a single production shoot, per details shared with Marketing Dive. Echo builds on a strategic partnership between Ogilvy parent WPP and Creative Artists Agency and operationalizes The CAA Vault, the talent agency’s system for capturing, storing and licensing digital likenesses of its clients.

Echo looks to solve for marketer needs around content creation while protecting talent rights and intellectual property. Traditional productions of advertising featuring celebrities and athletes — a $25 billion-dollar annual global market, per Ogilvy — increasingly do not meet the needs of always-on, digital-first campaigns. At the same time, brands and their ambassadors are working to meet consumer demands around trust in an ecosystem heavy with deepfakes and other unauthorized artificial intelligence-generated content.

“Clients want more content, and [talent agencies] have high quality assets. How do we bridge those things together?” said Carol Reed, global chief innovation officer at Ogilvy. “It's not about creating new software to sell to people. It is more about how you solve the question around human AI likeness and making it scalable and repeatable for wide-scale use.”

Echo, commercially available across the WPP network this month, is powered by WPP Open, the holding company’s AI-powered operating system that is at the heart of its modernized offering. The workflow begins with capturing voice and video as part of the CAA Vault process. Ogilvy then takes those models and creates storyboard elements and creative assets that are turned into ads, all with approval from client and talent.

The system allows for an asset shoot to generate 30 to 50 media-ready assets, rather than the eight to 10 yielded by traditional productions, reducing average cost-per-asset by an estimated 65% to 75%. But beyond cost effectiveness, investment optimization, contextual relevance and personalization, Reed wants clients to use Echo to think bigger, especially as creatives get more comfortable with AI tools.

“I don't want people to feel like we're cutting corners. It's about ideally unlocking impossible things,” she said. “Being able to have more ideas come out of it and not just variations is really exciting to me… We can land more creative ideas in impossible situations.”

Echo is designed to meet the needs of marketers, agencies and talent, but Ogilvy also validated the technology with consumers, surveying more than 1,200 respondents in the U.S., UK and India through a mix of intuitive association research methods and traditional survey methodology.

More than 80% of global respondents recognized talent-approved messaging as a cue of talent-approved AI usage — approval that strengthened ad appeal among more than 76% of global respondents. Even consumers generally skeptical of AI reported that explicit talent sign-off increased trust, credibility and reassurance.

“Trust in advertising has always come from two things: someone you believe and an idea worth believing. AI has challenged both,” David Raichman, executive creative director and global AI creative lead for The Ogilvy Group, said in a statement. “Echo puts them back together: the talent’s consent on every asset, and a creative idea strong enough to deserve it.”

Trust is built into Echo in several ways. Generated assets are automatically checked against machine-readable talent usage terms and brand safety guidelines, with assets unable to be released without final sign-off through an approval portal. AI models are trained only from CAA Vault data, and all cleared consumer-facing assets have a visible watermark in the format: “[Talent Name] Approved | Recreated with AI.”

“I actually didn't know what was going to come out of that research. I was a little nervous, to be honest with you, but I think trust is the main theme,” Reed said. “We're at a point now where people aren't afraid of AI. You see it in your feeds, and I think people are getting to the point where they appreciate disclosure and transparency.”

While Ogilvy would not reveal which advertisers or talent have used or plan to use Echo, Reed confirmed that pilots are in process.The manner in which talent, advertiser and creative agency can have conversations together, rather than separately, is a change which could require all parties to adjust.

“This technology creates this convergence of acknowledging what could be possible if we all aligned our ducks, and so that takes a little bit of time to find the right use case,” Reed said. “We never want to feel like we're using AI or technology for the sake of using it.”

#7299. Meta’s AI ads included unapproved discounts

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Recent reports found that the artificial intelligence-powered ad tools posted discount offers to customers even with promotions turned off.

As artificial intelligence tools become more empowered, new parameters need to be established to limit their capacity when it comes to undertaking certain tasks.

There have already been reports of an AI tool giving out a user’s home address, generating hundreds of videos at a users’ expense and conducting questionable crypto trades.

Automated errors can also extend to buying digital ads. PPC Land reported last week that Meta’s AI-powered ad tools took discounts from a store’s website and displayed them on the business’s Facebook and Instagram ads, “even when the shop had turned promotions off on the ad it copied.”

The discovery was made by digital marketing advisor Bram Van der Hallen, who shared a LinkedIn post outlining the discovery.

As per Van der Hallen: “Meta may now automatically detect offers from your website and use them in your Meta ads. Even when you have turned off this option for your original ad. When the option to display offers detected from your website and ads is enabled in Commerce Manager, Meta may then automatically display these offers in your ads.”

Van der Hallen said the issue can be controlled by updating Commerce Manager settings to stop Meta from using detected offers in other campaigns.

But this adds another element to consider, and PPC Land noted that it could cause issues for advertisers: “This matters for any business advertising on Meta with more than one offer live, because a discount meant for one campaign or one audience could show up somewhere else.”

Meta recently outlined how its expanded processing capacity is helping generate more effective ad campaigns. The company said that improvements to its ads ranking system drove a more than 8% increase in ad clicks and a 15.7% uplift in conversions on Facebook in Q2 2026.

However, as more systems are guided by AI, there will be errors because AI systems seek out efficiencies and optimizations wherever they can, which could cause issues.

Advertisers need to be aware of these potential issues, which could have a big impact on campaign approaches.

#7296. Pepsi’s holiday push includes bigger retail presence, soda for Santa

New ads expand on a “Food Deserves Pepsi” platform that launched in 2024 and positions the soft drink as the ideal pairing with food.

Pepsi is ramping up its marketing activity around the holiday and football seasons, two occasions with a strong connection to food, for efforts that build on a “Food Deserves Pepsi” platform that launched in 2024 and positions the soft drinks as an essential pairing with food. Other moments Pepsi has looked to plug itself into as part of the platform have included soccer viewing parties, barbecues and pizza delivery.

The TV spot will be amplified across a variety of channels and during key moments, including NBC’s holiday tree lighting programming, college football games on Christmas Eve and Christmas Day NBA and NFL games. Additionally, Pepsi expects to have 80% more visibility in retail locations over the year-ago period through holiday packaging, displays, inventory and customer-specific programming throughout the season.

A limited-edition Pepsi Vanilla & Cream Holiday Bundle will be available starting Nov. 19 on Walmart’s website and includes holiday baking items and Pepsi merchandise. Pepsi Vanilla & Cream launched Oct. 18 and has so far received a strong consumer reception, per the brand.

Tapping into football hype, Pepsi launched custom creative featuring Bettis on Nov. 4 across Walmart’s website and social channels. A video, titled “Flag on Flavor,” sees the NFL legend surprising Walmart shoppers while promoting a “Tailgating Deserves Pepsi” campaign. The effort will also be promoted across 15 NFL team partnerships via retail, new creative and in-person experiences.

Pepsi has deepened its connection to football via retail visibility, with a 30% increase in point-of-sale presence over last year, per the brand. Pepsi has been the official soft drink of the NFL for nearly three decades. Earlier this year, the brand advertised in the Super Bowl with a 30-second national spot that featured a polar bear who is befuddled after picking Pepsi Zero Sugar over Coke Zero in a blind taste test.

PepsiCo in Q3 saw net revenue increase 5.6%, per an earnings statement. For its beverages division, the company reported improving organic volume trends, driven by strength in energy drinks, functional hydration and zero-sugar and flavored soft drinks. Still, PepsiCo is looking to trim spending as its broader North American business continues to face sales challenges amid shifting consumer habits.

This fall, KFC U.S. announced that it will replace Pepsi beverages with Coca-Cola across its restaurant system by spring 2027. The win for rival Coke comes as its Mr. Pibb beverage rises as the fastest-growing brand this year. Another rival, Keurig Dr Pepper, is planning to increase its marketing investment, potentially presenting another challenge for PepsiCo.

Correction: This piece has been updated with the proper spelling of Pepsi’s Yes Chef Tailgates program.

#7293. YouTube expands custom feeds and offers new partnership options

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform is trying to make it easier for users to access personally relevant discovery options using artificial intelligence-enabled responses.

YouTube updated its in-app discovery listings and also integrated its artificial intelligence-powered Ask Studio guidance with its support tools to make it easier to manage queries in a single workflow. The company is also testing product recommendations for potential creator partnerships.

First, YouTube is expanding its custom feed listings in order to make it easier for users to create and access personally relevant feeds based on conversational prompts.

Currently available to U.S. users, YouTube’s custom feed generation option provides another way to define the in-app experience by enabling users to tell YouTube’s AI system what they want to see.

YouTube is now making these custom feeds easier to access by adding them to the top navigation bar.

These custom feeds will also replace non-custom topic options in the top listing. YouTube's also moving the subscription and standard feed options, bringing them together into the top-of-feed display.

That should make it easier for users to integrate this AI-powered option and help them build a more personally relevant in-app experience.

For creators, YouTube is rolling out an integrated Ask Studio and YouTube Help chat element. This should make it easier for creators to generate AI guidance for their channel and connect with YouTube’s internal support for other queries.

YouTube’s Head of Editorial Rene Ritchie said this will mean that creators no longer have to switch between chat windows for each element.

YouTube is also testing product recommendations for brand content partnerships. These are personalized to each channel and could help creators find more relevant sponsorship opportunities.

As explained by Ritchie: “If you're an eligible affiliate creator, YouTube Studio is rolling out a brand new personalized product recommendation shelf right inside your shopping hub. These recommendations are based on your channel's past content and audience engagement and what's trending in your niche, like beauty, tech, or home.”

The new display will also show estimated commission rates for each potential partnership, providing more assistance for creators when considering their opportunities.

Finally, YouTube is expanding its Hype with Jewels creator donation option to more markets.

This is a combination of two products: YouTube’s Jewels are essentially an in-app currency that viewers can use to buy in-app digital stickers, which they can then send to creators to show their support during a livestream.

Users can purchase packages of Jewels, and creators get a cut from any sticker allocated during their stream.

YouTube’s Hype program, meanwhile, enables viewers to allocate Hype points to a video in order to boost its ranking and help it get seen by more people.

Hype with Jewels lets creators use purchased Jewels to add more Hype to videos, which will then help them get seen by more people.

As per YouTube: “Starting November 6, 2026, we’re expanding Hype with Jewels to eligible creators and viewers in the United States, Canada, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom.”

YouTube is also expanding the Hype limits for streams, with viewers now able to allocate as much Hype as they like to streamers.

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

New functionality allows Meta’s artificial intelligence agent to store task trackers and convert commands into custom interfaces.

Meta added a new option to its Muse artificial intelligence agents that will enable users to create mini apps addressing whatever topic they choose.

As outlined by Alex Cornell, a product designer for Muse, Muse Spaces are dedicated commands converted into their own interface, which makes them easy to revisit for ongoing tracking.

To create a Space, Muse users tell the agent to create a Space based on whatever parameters they want.

Muse will then store these trackers as mini apps within the Muse sidebar.

That could make it easier to stay updated on whatever information the user chooses, with Meta providing a range of potential use cases:

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said that he had created a Muse Space that controls the vents on his meat smoker via Bluetooth.

As per Meta: “Got a half-finished idea sitting in your notes app, a spreadsheet you keep meaning to clean up, or a hobby you want to dive into? Chances are you can turn it into a space.”

The option could lead to some interesting use cases, and could help users streamline and improve their task management.

Meta also added expanded memory to Muse and Meta AI, which should better enable these AI tools to provide personalized responses based on advanced systematic understanding of each user.

Meta’s Active Memory and Active Focus features, which were originally announced as part of its Muse Wonder update, will extend the capacity of its AI tools to recall previously mentioned details in chats.

As per Meta: “Active Memory enables Muse and Meta AI to remember what matters and recognize when earlier information becomes relevant, making it easier to build off your past conversations. We’ve trained our models to recognize what type of information is temporary versus permanent, to reason across time, and to distinguish between what is still relevant and what has become stale.”

Active Focus, meanwhile, enables Meta’s Muse agents to continue working toward a goal, even if the agents are faced with unexpected challenges.

“We’ve trained our models on a variety of bottlenecks reflective of the real world, so that they can try harder, recover, or find alternatives on your behalf. In Muse, our models show a 67% improvement in completing everyday tasks where unexpected issues arise.”

That could help to ensure Muse gets more things done, though there have also been reports of empowered other AI agents breaking through system security measures to complete an assigned task.

As reported by Wired, OpenAI had to revise its containment measures recently after a set of rogue AI breached another company’s system.

Meta recently reported that the Muse app has already exceeded 10 million downloads, and that shopping was its primary use case.

Analysis from app data provider Sensor Tower, however, has shown that user retention for Muse dips significantly two weeks after download, which means that Meta will need to keep highlighting practical use cases to maintain interest in the app.

#7281. Meta expands age detection measures for teens

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company said it’s implementing more tools to help protect young users, and called on competitors to follow suit.

Meta announced on Monday that it’s expanding its use of its artificial intelligence-powered age estimation technology to ensure that more teens are placed into age-appropriate experiences. The move comes amid ongoing global discussions about teen social media restrictions.

Over the past year, Meta has been working to improve its age detection system, which utilizes visual and contextual analysis to determine a user’s age.

As explained by Meta: “We use AI technology to find people we suspect to be teens, even if they use an adult birthday, and place them in Teen Account protections. Since first introducing this technology, we’ve been placing more teens in age-appropriate protections and are encouraged by the results.”

Meta said that this process has ensured that millions of teens across the world are placed into protective experiences, even when teens misrepresent their age.

“We’re continuing to roll this technology out on Facebook and, later this year, we’ll begin launching similar technology globally on Threads,” Meta said. “This expansion builds on our commitments under our recent agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general to strengthen how we identify teens and children under 13 on our apps.”

In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion and implement a range of new teen protection measures to settle a landmark lawsuit brought by a coalition of U.S. attorneys general. By settling the case, Meta avoided a trial, which could have put a spotlight on the harms caused by social media.

Some of the measures Meta agreed to implement as part of this settlement included time limits on teen social media usage, blocks on notifications during school times and overnight and the capacity for teen users to set a non-algorithmic feed as the default.

Meta has implemented these measures yet, but as more regions consider similar restrictions, the company appears to want to get out in front of any demands, in order to present itself as taking proactive action.

But Meta would probably not be taking these steps if not for the U.S. attorneys general’s case.

The bigger question, however, is just how effective the company’s automated account estimation and teen detection tools will be. While Meta is keen to highlight the potential here, evidence suggests that this new push won’t be as effective as the company is claiming.

In Australia, for example, Meta said it removed more than 750,000 profiles it detected as belonging to teen users. That move was part of the company’s compliance with Australia’s social media ban for users under age 16, which went into effect in December 2025.

That’s a significant amount. However, a report from Australia’s eSafety Commission published in August indicated that 81.5% of underage users continued to access restricted apps.

That suggests that either Meta’s detection systems are not as effective as the company claims, or teens are simply finding new ways to evade detection.

On Monday, Meta also announced an Australia-specific measure that will see the company incorporateApple’s age-range signal as another means to determine user age.

“The process is simple,” Meta said. “When a parent sets up a smartphone for their teen, they have the option for the app store to confirm the age of the person using the device and assign them an age range. Then, each time the teen downloads an app, Apple passes that age range to the developer — Meta, for example — confirming whether the teen meets the app’s age requirement.”

Meta said it’s voluntarily using this information, while also reiterating its call for app stores to play a bigger role in determining user age at the download level.

Finally, Meta used Monday’s announcement as an opportunity to deflect some of the pressure it’s been under regarding age checking by calling on other platforms to implement similar protections.

“We’ll continue to do our part to proactively ensure teens are in age-appropriate experiences on our apps,” Meta said. “That’s why as part of our agreement with 52 bipartisan attorneys general across US states, territories, and the District of Columbia, we’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to children under 13. We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may belong to teens between the ages of 13 and 17 so we can ensure those accounts are placed in experiences designed for teens, even if they give us an adult birthday. As Instagram is just one of the many apps teens use, we’re also calling on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to adopt these same practices to keep teens safe.”

It seems like a questionable approach, using the critically important issue of protecting teen users as corporate leverage.

But that's the angle that Meta's going with, as it seeks to dilute the potential impact of such changes on its business.

#7279. Why Rao’s heated up brand building with a request to slow down meals

The Campbell Company sauce brand reimagines the concept of a limited-time offer by keying in on how many meals people have left with loved ones.

Rao’s Homemade today revealed a four-minute short film that reimagines the concept of a limited-time offer by reminding consumers that the most limited time is the time people spend together, per details shared with Marketing Dive. “Limited-Time Only” was directed by Aqsa Altaf and John X. Carey, the duo known as Aqsa + John X. who were behind Dove’s “Real Beauty Sketches” campaign.

“Limited-Time Only” shares the story of three individuals as they are interviewed about how often they have dinner with family. The heart-tugging video culminates with each being presented a jar of Rao’s sauce labeled with an estimate of how many meals they have left with certain family members before being surprised with a dinner with their loved ones.

The short film is part of a larger “Make Time” campaign created with Goodby Silverstein & Partners that spans premium video, social, influencer, public relations, retail media and owned channels.

In a survey of more than 1,000 individuals and in-depth interviews with 200 people, the brand and agency learned that 84% of Americans wish they shared more meals with loved ones, yet only one-third of families actually sit down together. The campaign unites those findings with product truths about the time-intensive way Rao’s sauce is made, from hand-picked tomatoes and hand-peeled onions and garlic that are simmered for hours.

“It's not just about the food; It's about the experience that creating that food enables, and it's an opportunity to really slow down and savor the food and to savor those that you're sitting around the table with, and to make meal time less of a transaction and more of an experience and an opportunity to connect with others,” said Chris Tutor, vice president of advertising and design at Rao’s parent The Campbell Company.

That experience was captured in a series of ads that feature groups of people enjoying a meal and include taglines like “the best part of the day is sharing it” and “keep long stories long.” The spots are set to live orchestral music and end with a scarpetta, the Italian tradition of using bread to mop up the last of the sauce. The creation of those spots led the team to investigate the larger narrative around meals with loved ones that informed “Limited-Time Only.”

“The long-form [video] allowed us to tell more of that story from the impetus for it to the aha moment to then the celebratory moment, and it really allowed us to blow out that visceral moment around the table into the full story,” Tutor said.

While “Limited-Time Only” does not have a traditional ad length, the creative is in line with a trend around longer-form content that marketers have adopted to tell more engaging stories to consumers. Depending on the platform, the brand will either run the long-form asset or teasers that point to the full video.

“There's been a lot of media attention around this idea, and so we’re leveraging media partners to help tell the story,” Tutor said. “Setting up the context before watching the film will also, we think, drive a lot of eyeballs to it. We're trying to do the math and science of making sure the right piece of content shows up on the right channel at the right time.”

The Campbell Company acquired Rao’s parent Sovos Brands for $2.7 billion deal in March 2024. Rao’s is a billion-dollar brand for Campbell’s and continues to grow, with consumption up 11.3% in fiscal year 2026. To fuel this growth, Rao’s increased media spending and will further increase it in fiscal 2027, executives said on a recent earnings call.

While Rao’s has grown household penetration, it still lags behind sister brand Prego. The “Make Time” campaign is key to the brand’s marketing efforts and represents both a brand building story and an awareness play.

“As people become aware of the brand or if they're already aware of the brand, what does the brand stand for beyond just that exceptional food? It's bringing this notion of slow living to every meal, reminding people that life tastes better when it's savored, and establishing what the brand means on an emotional level, versus just a rational level,” Tutor said.

#7275. Instagram launches visual effects creator for Edits

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The new tool allows users to describe and build effects without the need for coding, and all approved effects will be available for public use in Instagram Stories.

Instagram has launched a web-based, artificial intelligence-powered effects builder option as part of its Edits platform, which will enable users to create and share digital effects for use in Instagram Stories.

The new element of Edits, called Effect Builder, works on conversational prompts, with users able to describe the visual effect they want. The tool will then be able to build it, no coding skills required.

As explained by Instagram product designer Cheechee Lin: “We've seen how much people love Restyle effects in Stories and how quickly a great effect takes off when it's easy to try. But until now, building effects required special design and technical skills. Now with Effect Builder, you don't need design or coding skills, or prior experience making effects. Describe the look you want, preview it on your own photos, and publish.”

As shown in this example screen, the Effect Builder process will provide a range of editable fields and elements, which users can change and refine as they go about building their effect.

Meta also said that images can be used as a style reference “to guide the look of your effect.”

“On the homepage’s prompt box, click Style reference to upload a photo,” Meta said. “Meta AI uses aspects of the image like its color, lighting and texture, to guide the look of your effect.”

Users can also test their effects in the editor to help customize and improve the output.

Once submitted, creator effects will be reviewed by Meta for safety before being made available for anyone else to use on Instagram.

Creators can check in on the status of their in-review effects in the Library tab in Effects Builder, and Meta’s review process will generally take less than 24 hours.

Once an effect is published, it will be available in the Stories effects browser alongside all other Stories effects. Lin said that user-created effects will include a link back to the effect creator’s profile.

The process is essentially an effects extension of the AI Restyle option that Instagram launched in October 2025, which also enabled users to generate visual effects via conversational prompts.

Effects created through that process could also be shared with others, so functionally, this new Effect Builder process is not new. But it does now seem to incorporate more creative elements. Meanwhile, the capacity to build effects via desktop could also lead to more complex, interesting creations.

Edits launched for MacOS last week. It’s the first step in the app’s expansion to desktop and this web-based Effects Builder is another part of that.

Maybe that will lead to more interesting uses of Meta’s AI tools for visual effects in Stories.

#7273. Synthetic audiences fall short: What marketers need to know

The AI-generated audience simulations may make it more difficult for brands to reach new audiences, writes RYA co-founder Mark Himmelsbach.

The following is a guest piece written by Mark Himmelsbach, co-founder of creative AI marketing tool RYA and advertising agency Episode Four. Opinions are the author’s own.

Artificial intelligence has proposed a novel technique for testing that’s cheaper, faster and whose proponents say is as accurate — perhaps even more so — as “real” research: synthetic audiences.

CMOs have good reasons to want this. Research is expensive, deadlines are short, marketers need to do even more with less and they increasingly need to justify their decisions using data. Synthetic audiences are simulated panels of customers, built from a set of data like customer records, interviews, demographic descriptions or combinations of those inputs.

These simulations can evaluate campaigns and explain their preferences in minutes. Marketers can then revise their work, ask again and repeat at a fraction of the cost of recruiting a human panel. But do synthetic audiences constitute high enough quality evidence?

The market seems to think so. In July, synthetic data company Simile raised $200 million at a $2 billion valuation, five months after announcing its series A. Even Adobe now lets marketers test creative, messaging and more against AI-generated customer profiles inside its Brand Intelligence product.

Now, properly identifying a target audience and codifying their preferences is hard enough. A simulation whose predictions hold up against real customer responses can help improve familiar campaigns. Indeed, for those teams who’ve successfully modeled their customers, synthetic audiences will save them considerable amounts of time and money.

There may even be additional creative possibilities on the margin — think more precise demographics, more targeted campaigns — but it basically helps you do more of the same.

A brand trying to acquire new customers, however, needs to understand people who haven’t yet made a decision to spend money with them. This is where simulations get tricky.

Synthetic audiences are being sold with that kind of solution in mind as well. Evidenza, for example, markets itself as “AI market research for impossible audiences,” as in impossible to do without AI.

But synthetic audiences still need evidence about the people they’re supposed to represent. Giving the model good evidence upon which to train is called grounding in the AI industry. For example, Bain reports that pairing simulated customers with a company’s own customer data substantially improved their overall performance.

But whose data are we talking about? What separates a useful synthetic audience from a generic simulation is data quality over time: whose experiences are represented, how recently were they observed, how relevant are they to the task at hand, and how often does new evidence get added to the training data?

A detailed snapshot of your existing customers may not actually provide much insight into potential customers who considered your brand but walked away. I’m reminded of the classic financial services industry disclosure: “past performance is not indicative of future results.”

Synthetic audiences – and synthetic data writ large – propose to use statistics and AI to create the data required to model those missed customers using external sources and observations. But again, part of the art of marketing is identifying trends and finding creative ways to stand out by doing something different that appeals to your target audience.

Whether or not AI can help humans do so is the trillion-dollar question.

Activision CMO Tyler Bahl, for example, asks what his team could do that only “Call of Duty” could do. His “stature, swagger, and scale” criteria express an ambition for the brand to delight their customers with singular, spirited ideas. A synthetic audience can help test how an idea might land, but can it decide what’s worth trying and how far to push it?

What’s more, there’s a self-reinforcing dynamic here that must be considered. Even if the data is high quality, and even if the model itself isn’t overtly biased, how might it eventually condition its users to test ideas likely to get accepted?

Constant scoring risks making a team more conservative and risk-averse rather than more creative and productive.

If campaigns need good “scores” to get approved, marketers will have every reason to learn what the panel rewards. This is commonly known as survivorship bias.

Under pressure, marketers may — consciously or not — begin incorporating those preferences before proposing something. Eventually, the process might invert: whereas the simulation was intended to improve creative decision-making, it may begin to influence creative decision-making, often regressing to the mean.

In the end, CMOs have to decide how much authority to give these tools, and leave their teams room to both use these models and pursue ideas the models wouldn’t have picked. They can thus derive considerable value from synthetic audiences while preserving the judgment and imagination that make their teams valuable. A few practical recommendations:

Cheaper, faster research should undoubtedly give creative teams more room to explore. Use simulation to test more ideas, learn from the results and improve the work. But marketing leaders must refrain from delegating too much of the process to the machines and remember to seek ways to ground their simulations in reality.

#7272. LinkedIn explains its improved content recommendation system

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company’s Profile Relevance model uses LLM-generated embeddings to show users more relevant posts from people they don’t follow.

LinkedIn shared insights into its evolving content recommendation system, with an overview of its improved, artificial intelligence-powered process. The platform’s system determines what content from non-connections gets displayed to users in their feed.

In a post on the LinkedIn Engineering Blog, LinkedIn engineer Shiyong Lin explained the platform’s new Profile Relevance model, which uses LLM-generated embeddings to match members and posts, based on professional context.

The process essentially summarizes each user’s profile into a prompt, taking into account each member’s profile information and posting history. It then builds a personalized guide of what they’re likely to be interested in.

On a basic level, this means that the system creates a chatbot-style summary of each user’s information, which then dictates what they get shown in the app.

Using these generated summaries, LinkedIn built a new recommendation system that measures content relevance versus each member’s summary.

As per Lin: “The system evaluates how well each post matches a member’s professional context across specific factors, including topic, location, job title, company, industry, seniority, and education.”

LinkedIn assessed these results manually before building a system that showed users more relevant posts from members they don’t follow in the app.

This has led to notable improvements in feed relevance.

As per Lin: “Online experiments recorded a +0.54% lift in Feed Updates Viewed, a +0.94% increase in viral rate, and a -18.8% reduction in hide rate, indicating a more relevant and less noisy member experience. For members, this translates into a feed that surfaces high-quality content beyond their immediate network while remaining aligned with their professional context, even when they have limited historical activity.”

Lin said that this system will also benefit creators by ensuring that their posts will reach relevant audiences beyond their immediate network.

“Notably, for cold-start members with limited activity history, we observed a +17.7% increase in viral engagement and a +1.8% lift in DAU, underscoring the model’s ability to generalize effectively even with sparse interaction data.”

In summary, the post recommendations from non-connections in the LinkedIn feed are likely now more relevant and more valuable, driving a better LinkedIn experience.

#7271. Engineering Manager, Automation Intelligence at Fingerprint

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.

We have raised $77M and are backed by Craft Ventures (Tesla, Facebook, Airbnb ), Nexus Venture Partners ( Postman, Apollo.io, MinIO, Druva) and Uncorrelated Ventures ( Redis, Rollbar,  Gradle).

Fingerprint's device intelligence platform processes billions of identification events for companies that need to know who — or what — is on the other end of a request. Increasingly, the answer is not a person. AI agents, AI assistants, crawlers, headless browsers, and malicious automation now make up a large and fast-growing share of internet traffic, and telling them apart from humans — and from each other — is becoming one of the most important problems our customers ask us to solve.

We are standing up a dedicated Automation Intelligence engineering team to own that problem end to end: detection in the browser, detection at the edge, the classification taxonomy that tells customers what kind of automation they're seeing and how confident we are, and the API that customers and their agents call.

We're looking for an Engineering Manager to lead this team. You'll inherit a small, senior group (three engineers to start, growing to four or five) and a clear mandate. You report directly to the VP of Engineering.

This is a hands-on-adjacent engineering manager role for a small, senior, high-leverage team. You are not expected to write the production code — your engineers and their agents do that — but you are expected to be close enough to it to set direction, evaluate the work, and hold the quality bar.

The team has unusual autonomy and unusual visibility. It owns a product that leadership considers strategically critical, it is the first team operating Fingerprint's AI-native engineering model, and its results — good and bad — will be used as evidence for how the rest of engineering works. That means two things: you'll have real room to decide how the team operates, and you'll need to be honest about what the data shows.

In the first 90 days you will likely: finalize the roster and ownership lines with the sibling team, get the quality loop and engineering baselines running, deliver the engineering evidence for the Beta gate, and run the first review of the AI-native operating model.

At Fingerprint, we believe in pay transparency — it's part of how we operate as a distributed, remote-first team.  Salaries are based on function, level, and geographic location, benchmarked against similar stage growth companies.

#7266. Senior Manager, Application Security at Fingerprint

Fingerprint empowers enterprises to detect and stop online fraud with the world’s most accurate device intelligence.  We lead our industry with bleeding-edge identification capabilities and work on turning new ideas and discoveries in the fraud detection space into reality. Our customers range from innovative startups to leading enterprise companies, including Plaid, Dropbox, and Booking.com.

Fingerprint is a globally dispersed, 100% remote company. We were named on on the 2026 Forbes Best Startup Employers list and ranked #803 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies.
